docs.text: ThermalFEA ¶ ThermalFEA is a desktop program for two-dimensional steady-state and transient heat conduction by the finite-element method. You draw or import a geometry, mesh it, apply loads and boundary conditions, solve, and look at the results. Everything the program does in the window can also be done from a Python script or the command line. This guide is for an engineer who has used a finite-element program before but has not seen this one. What the program does ¶ Analysis: steady-state and transient, linear and nonlinear (temperature-dependent properties, radiation, convection correlations). Models: planar models (with a thickness per region) and axisymmetric models (x is the radius, y is the axis). Elements: 3-node and 6-node triangles, 4-node and 8-node quadrilaterals. Materials: isotropic or orthotropic conductivity, density and specific heat, each constant or a table against temperature. A built-in library of solids and fluids is included ( Materials ). Geometry: points, lines, arcs, circles, rectangles, polygons and splines; union, cut and intersect; translate, rotate, mirror and scale; import of STEP, BREP and DXF files. Meshing: free meshing with triangles or quad-dominant meshes, structured meshing, size control, linear or quadratic elements and a quality report. Meshing uses gmsh. Loads and boundary conditions: fixed temperature, heat flux, heat flow in watts, volumetric heat generation, convection (a given coefficient, or a coefficient from a correlation), radiation to the ambient, thermal contact resistance and initial conditions. A load value may be a constant, a table against time, or an expression of time, position and temperature. Convection library: forced and natural convection correlations for plates, cylinders and ducts, with temperature-dependent fluid properties ( Correlations ). Flow solver: one-dimensional streams and pipe networks. From a given flow rate the program computes velocity, Reynolds number, heat-transfer coefficient, pressure drop and the rise of the fluid temperature along the wall, coupled to the solid. Post-processing: contour and vector plots, nodal temperature against time, plots along a path, probes, minimum and maximum, reaction heat flows, the energy balance, animation, and export to CSV, VTK (ParaView) and PNG. Files: the model is a JSON file ( .tfea ); results are stored beside it in an HDF5 file ( <model>.tfea.h5 ). What the program does not do ¶ No three-dimensional analysis, no flow simulation (CFD), no structural or thermal-stress coupling, no other physics, no radiation through participating media, no parallel solving. Enclosure (surface-to-surface) radiation, phase change (latent heat) and the HTML report are not available in this version; they are on hold. There is no packaged Windows installer yet. Limitations lists these and the smaller known gaps in one place. Map of the guide ¶ Page What it holds Installation Requirements, installing, starting the program, the command line Getting started The workflow in the window and from the command line Tutorials NAFEMS T4 steady plate , transient quench of a fin , cold plate with a water stream Examples Main closure of a canned-motor pump : an axisymmetric assembly with contacts, heat-up, steady state and a parameter study Units The unit systems and what they change Materials The built-in material library Correlations Every convection correlation, with its validity range Theory Every equation the program implements Verification The benchmark cases the program is checked against and their tolerances Limitations What is not available or not yet reviewed The pages Units, Materials, Correlations, Theory and Verification are generated from the project's own documents and code, so they cannot drift from what the program does. Conventions in this guide ¶ Values are SI (metres, seconds, kelvin, watts) unless a page says otherwise. The program can show other units; see Units . Files always store SI. A heat flow is reported as positive when heat enters the body. Menu entries are written as in the program, for example File > Examples.

Validity ranges and warnings ¶ For the horizontal-plate pair, pick "up" or "down" automatically at run time from the sign of (T_s − T∞) and the declared face direction. Outside a validity range: still evaluate, and emit one warning per boundary condition per solve. plate_forced_local needs the leading-edge point and flow direction; x is the distance of the integration point from the leading edge along the flow direction (minimum x = 1e-6 m). inclined_natural : when the face direction is declared, a face for which [I] makes no recommendation counts as outside the validity range: the top face ( up ) of a hot plate (T_s > T∞), or the bottom face ( down ) of a cold plate. When no face direction is declared, this is not checked. Characteristic lengths in a 2D model. Horizontal plates. [I] defines L = A_s/P (Eq. 9.29). In a planar model a horizontal face is a strip of unit depth, so A_s/P is half the strip's width; [I] Example 9.3 uses w/2 in the same way. In an axisymmetric model, a horizontal ring from r_i to r_o gives A_s/P = (r_o − r_i)/2. Either way, the automatic L_c of hplate_up_natural and hplate_down_natural is half the total length of the selection . This settles Q17.2. Other correlations. For the other plate correlations and the vertical channels (channel height), the automatic L_c is the total length of the selection. Diameters. The cylinder, sphere and non-circular cylinder correlations need L_c (the diameter or D) given. An explicit L_c always overrides the automatic one. Extra inputs (Data §8 params ): Vertical channels: S , the plate spacing [m]. slot_jet : W , the slot width [m]; H , the nozzle-to-surface distance [m]; x_r , the half-width of the region averaged over [m]. The default x_r is half the total length of the selection. round_jet : D , the nozzle diameter [m]; H [m]; r_r , the radius of the region averaged over [m]. In an axisymmetric model the default r_r is the largest radial coordinate of the selection; a planar model must give r_r . The jets take their L_c from these inputs , so a given L_c is refused. Internal duct flow, friction factor and pressure drop (Theory §8.1) ¶ This is the text of §8.1 of the theory document, unchanged. It holds the laminar Nusselt numbers, the turbulent and transition relations, the optional Dittus–Boelter relation, the Churchill friction factor and the pressure drop of a duct. Re = ṁ D_h /(A μ), D_h = 4A/P_wet. Properties at the bulk fluid temperature. Laminar (Re ≤ 2300): Nu_lam from the tables below ([I] Tables 8.1 and 8.2). Turbulent (Re ≥ 4000): Gnielinski ([I] 8.62, with f from 8.21) Nu = (f/8)(Re − 1000) Pr / [1 + 12.7 (f/8)^½ (Pr^⅔ − 1)], f = (0.790 ln Re − 1.64)⁻² (valid 0.5 ≤ Pr ≤ 2000, 3000 ≤ Re ≤ 5e6). Transition (2300 < Re < 4000): linear interpolation in Re between Nu_lam and Nu_Gnielinski(Re = 4000). [I] gives no transition correlation; this rule is the program's. Cross-section ( cross_section ) Nu_lam, constant wall T Nu_lam, constant flux Circular ( circular ) 3.66 4.36 Parallel plates, both heated ( parallel_plates ) 7.54 8.23 Parallel plates, one side insulated ( parallel_plates_one_side ) 4.86 5.39 Square ( square ) 2.98 3.61 Rectangle, sides b/a = 1.43 ( rectangle_1_43 ) 3.08 3.73 Rectangle, b/a = 2.0 ( rectangle_2 ) 3.39 4.12 Rectangle, b/a = 3.0 ( rectangle_3 ) 3.96 4.79 Rectangle, b/a = 4.0 ( rectangle_4 ) 4.44 5.33 Rectangle, b/a = 8.0 ( rectangle_8 ) 5.60 6.49 Triangle ( triangle ) 2.49 3.11 Concentric annulus , one surface at constant temperature and the other insulated ([I] Table 8.2). D_h = D_o − D_i. The stream gives diameter_ratio = D_i/D_o. Nu is linearly interpolated in D_i/D_o between the rows; the program, not [I], sets that rule. D_i/D_o Nu_i: inner surface heated ( annulus_inner ) Nu_o: outer surface heated ( annulus_outer ) 0 — 3.66 0.05 17.46 4.06 0.10 11.56 4.11 0.25 7.37 4.23 0.50 5.74 4.43 1.00 4.86 4.86 annulus_inner needs 0.05 ≤ D_i/D_o ≤ 1. annulus_outer needs 0 ≤ D_i/D_o ≤ 1. [I] gives only constant-temperature values for the annulus, so a constant-flux request is refused. Default is the constant-wall-temperature value. Optional user selections, each replacing Gnielinski as the turbulent formula (the laminar value and the transition rule are kept): Dittus–Boelter ([I] 8.60): Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^n. n = 0.4 if the wall is hotter than the fluid, else 0.3. Valid for 0.6 ≤ Pr ≤ 160 and Re ≥ 1e4. Sieder–Tate ([I] 8.61): Nu = 0.027 Re^(4/5) Pr^(1/3) (μ/μ_s)^0.14. μ_s is taken at the cell's mean wall temperature T̄_w; the other properties at the bulk temperature. Valid for 0.7 ≤ Pr ≤ 16700 and Re ≥ 1e4. [I] recommends it for flows with large property variation, such as oils. Friction factor, all regimes (Churchill 1977, not in [I]), roughness e: f = 8 [ (8/Re)¹² + (A + B)^(−1.5) ]^(1/12), A = [2.457 ln( 1 / ((7/Re)^0.9 + 0.27 e/D_h) )]¹⁶, B = (37530/Re)¹⁶ Pressure drop of a duct of length L with minor-loss coefficient K_minor: Δp = (f L/D_h + K_minor) · ρ V²/2, V = ṁ/(ρ A). §8.2 Correlations of [I] that are not used ¶ Recorded so that no task adds them without a decision. On 2026-11-23 the owner judged the correlations in use adequate and declined the enclosure, mixed-convection and Table 8.1 f·Re additions (Q30.4): Circular cylinder, Hilpert ([I] 7.52, Table 7.2) and Zukauskas (7.53). These cover the same case as Churchill–Bernstein (7.54), which is kept. Horizontal cylinder, Morgan (9.33, Table 9.1) is not used either; Churchill–Chu (9.34) is kept. Liquid-metal forms : the flat plate (7.32) and fully developed tube flow (8.64, 8.65). Mercury is the only liquid metal built in. Other correlations used outside their Pr range warn as usual. Flat plate with uniform surface flux (7.45–7.48) or an unheated starting length (7.60–7.64). The surface conditions these assume are not known to a load. Tube banks (7.58, 7.59), packed beds (7.81), falling drops (7.57), and arrays of jets (7.73, 7.77). These need array geometry and a mean fluid temperature that a single-surface load does not have. Laminar entry lengths (8.57, 8.58). These give a Nusselt number averaged from the inlet to x, but the stream needs a local value in each cell. Colebrook friction (8.20) and laminar f·Re of non-circular sections (Table 8.1). Churchill 1977 is kept; it applies to circular ducts and to D_h. Using Table 8.1's f·Re would need a rule for joining it to the turbulent branch, which [I] does not give (OPEN_QUESTIONS Q30). Isoflux vertical channels (9.46), inclined channels (9.47), and the isolated-plate optimum spacings (Table 9.3). The isothermal form 9.45 is used. Enclosures: rectangular cavities, concentric cylinders and spheres (9.49–9.63). They couple two surfaces across a cavity, and a convection load sees only one ambient temperature (Q30). Mixed free and forced convection (9.64). This needs two correlations in one load (Q30). Boiling and condensation (chapter 10). The fluids here do not change phase. The stream and network equations that use these relations are in Theory §9 . Literature sources ¶ Every correlation except the user power law comes from Bergman, Lavine, Incropera and DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer , 7th ed., Wiley, 2011; each entry above gives its equation numbers. The Churchill friction factor (1977) is not in that book. The correlations of the book that the program does not use, and why, are listed in Theory §8.2 .

The equation numbers below are the book's (owner's decision, 2026-11-23). h = Nu · k_f / L_c. Fluid properties at the film temperature T_film = (T_s + T∞)/2 unless the correlation states otherwise. T_s is the wall temperature of the previous nonlinear iteration (lagged), either local (at each integration point; default) or the area average over the boundary set (option). docs.text: For the horizontal-plate pair, pick "up" or "down" automatically at run time from the sign of (T_s − T∞) and the declared face direction. Outside a validity range: still evaluate, and emit one warning per boundary condition per solve. plate_forced_local needs the leading-edge point and flow direction; x is the distance of the integration point from the leading edge along the flow direction (minimum x = 1e-6 m). inclined_natural : when the face direction is declared, a face for which [I] makes no recommendation counts as outside the validity range: the top face ( up ) of a hot plate (T_s > T∞), or the bottom face ( down ) of a cold plate. When no face direction is declared, this is not checked. Characteristic lengths in a 2D model. Horizontal plates. [I] defines L = A_s/P (Eq. 9.29). In a planar model a horizontal face is a strip of unit depth, so A_s/P is half the strip's width; [I] Example 9.3 uses w/2 in the same way. In an axisymmetric model, a horizontal ring from r_i to r_o gives A_s/P = (r_o − r_i)/2. Either way, the automatic L_c of hplate_up_natural and hplate_down_natural is half the total length of the selection . This settles Q17.2. Other correlations. For the other plate correlations and the vertical channels (channel height), the automatic L_c is the total length of the selection. Diameters. The cylinder, sphere and non-circular cylinder correlations need L_c (the diameter or D) given. An explicit L_c always overrides the automatic one. Extra inputs (Data §8 params ): Vertical channels: S , the plate spacing [m]. slot_jet : W , the slot width [m]; H , the nozzle-to-surface distance [m]; x_r , the half-width of the region averaged over [m]. The default x_r is half the total length of the selection. round_jet : D , the nozzle diameter [m]; H [m]; r_r , the radius of the region averaged over [m]. In an axisymmetric model the default r_r is the largest radial coordinate of the selection; a planar model must give r_r . The jets take their L_c from these inputs , so a given L_c is refused.

docs.text: This is the text of §8.1 of the theory document, unchanged. It holds the laminar Nusselt numbers, the turbulent and transition relations, the optional Dittus–Boelter relation, the Churchill friction factor and the pressure drop of a duct. Re = ṁ D_h /(A μ), D_h = 4A/P_wet. Properties at the bulk fluid temperature. Laminar (Re ≤ 2300): Nu_lam from the tables below ([I] Tables 8.1 and 8.2). Turbulent (Re ≥ 4000): Gnielinski ([I] 8.62, with f from 8.21) Nu = (f/8)(Re − 1000) Pr / [1 + 12.7 (f/8)^½ (Pr^⅔ − 1)], f = (0.790 ln Re − 1.64)⁻² (valid 0.5 ≤ Pr ≤ 2000, 3000 ≤ Re ≤ 5e6). Transition (2300 < Re < 4000): linear interpolation in Re between Nu_lam and Nu_Gnielinski(Re = 4000). [I] gives no transition correlation; this rule is the program's. Cross-section ( cross_section ) Nu_lam, constant wall T Nu_lam, constant flux Circular ( circular ) 3.66 4.36 Parallel plates, both heated ( parallel_plates ) 7.54 8.23 Parallel plates, one side insulated ( parallel_plates_one_side ) 4.86 5.39 Square ( square ) 2.98 3.61 Rectangle, sides b/a = 1.43 ( rectangle_1_43 ) 3.08 3.73 Rectangle, b/a = 2.0 ( rectangle_2 ) 3.39 4.12 Rectangle, b/a = 3.0 ( rectangle_3 ) 3.96 4.79 Rectangle, b/a = 4.0 ( rectangle_4 ) 4.44 5.33 Rectangle, b/a = 8.0 ( rectangle_8 ) 5.60 6.49 Triangle ( triangle ) 2.49 3.11 Concentric annulus , one surface at constant temperature and the other insulated ([I] Table 8.2). D_h = D_o − D_i. The stream gives diameter_ratio = D_i/D_o. Nu is linearly interpolated in D_i/D_o between the rows; the program, not [I], sets that rule. D_i/D_o Nu_i: inner surface heated ( annulus_inner ) Nu_o: outer surface heated ( annulus_outer ) 0 — 3.66 0.05 17.46 4.06 0.10 11.56 4.11 0.25 7.37 4.23 0.50 5.74 4.43 1.00 4.86 4.86 annulus_inner needs 0.05 ≤ D_i/D_o ≤ 1. annulus_outer needs 0 ≤ D_i/D_o ≤ 1. [I] gives only constant-temperature values for the annulus, so a constant-flux request is refused. Default is the constant-wall-temperature value. Optional user selections, each replacing Gnielinski as the turbulent formula (the laminar value and the transition rule are kept): Dittus–Boelter ([I] 8.60): Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^n. n = 0.4 if the wall is hotter than the fluid, else 0.3. Valid for 0.6 ≤ Pr ≤ 160 and Re ≥ 1e4. Sieder–Tate ([I] 8.61): Nu = 0.027 Re^(4/5) Pr^(1/3) (μ/μ_s)^0.14. μ_s is taken at the cell's mean wall temperature T̄_w; the other properties at the bulk temperature. Valid for 0.7 ≤ Pr ≤ 16700 and Re ≥ 1e4. [I] recommends it for flows with large property variation, such as oils. Friction factor, all regimes (Churchill 1977, not in [I]), roughness e: f = 8 [ (8/Re)¹² + (A + B)^(−1.5) ]^(1/12), A = [2.457 ln( 1 / ((7/Re)^0.9 + 0.27 e/D_h) )]¹⁶, B = (37530/Re)¹⁶ Pressure drop of a duct of length L with minor-loss coefficient K_minor: Δp = (f L/D_h + K_minor) · ρ V²/2, V = ṁ/(ρ A).
docs.title: Internal duct flow, friction factor and pressure drop (Theory §8.1)

docs.text: Recorded so that no task adds them without a decision. On 2026-11-23 the owner judged the correlations in use adequate and declined the enclosure, mixed-convection and Table 8.1 f·Re additions (Q30.4): Circular cylinder, Hilpert ([I] 7.52, Table 7.2) and Zukauskas (7.53). These cover the same case as Churchill–Bernstein (7.54), which is kept. Horizontal cylinder, Morgan (9.33, Table 9.1) is not used either; Churchill–Chu (9.34) is kept. Liquid-metal forms : the flat plate (7.32) and fully developed tube flow (8.64, 8.65). Mercury is the only liquid metal built in. Other correlations used outside their Pr range warn as usual. Flat plate with uniform surface flux (7.45–7.48) or an unheated starting length (7.60–7.64). The surface conditions these assume are not known to a load. Tube banks (7.58, 7.59), packed beds (7.81), falling drops (7.57), and arrays of jets (7.73, 7.77). These need array geometry and a mean fluid temperature that a single-surface load does not have. Laminar entry lengths (8.57, 8.58). These give a Nusselt number averaged from the inlet to x, but the stream needs a local value in each cell. Colebrook friction (8.20) and laminar f·Re of non-circular sections (Table 8.1). Churchill 1977 is kept; it applies to circular ducts and to D_h. Using Table 8.1's f·Re would need a rule for joining it to the turbulent branch, which [I] does not give (OPEN_QUESTIONS Q30). Isoflux vertical channels (9.46), inclined channels (9.47), and the isolated-plate optimum spacings (Table 9.3). The isothermal form 9.45 is used. Enclosures: rectangular cavities, concentric cylinders and spheres (9.49–9.63). They couple two surfaces across a cavity, and a convection load sees only one ambient temperature (Q30). Mixed free and forced convection (9.64). This needs two correlations in one load (Q30). Boiling and condensation (chapter 10). The fluids here do not change phase. The stream and network equations that use these relations are in Theory §9 .
docs.title: §8.2 Correlations of [I] that are not used

docs.text: Every correlation except the user power law comes from Bergman, Lavine, Incropera and DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer , 7th ed., Wiley, 2011; each entry above gives its equation numbers. The Churchill friction factor (1977) is not in that book. The correlations of the book that the program does not use, and why, are listed in Theory §8.2 .

docs.text: Getting started ¶ This page describes the workflow as the program presents it, first in the window and then from the command line and from Python. The tutorials apply it to worked problems. The program has not yet been reviewed on a real screen by its owner (see Limitations ). Layout and wording of the window may change. The window ¶ Start the program as described in Installation . Model dock (top left): the model tree. Properties dock (below it): the panel of the item selected in the tree. Viewport (centre): the geometry, the mesh, load symbols and result plots. Messages dock (bottom): the solver log. An Issues dock is tabbed with it and lists the findings of validation. The View menu shows and hides the docks, and switches the load symbols on and off ("Load symbols"). Toolbar : the selection modes None, Point, Curve, Surface, Node and Element, and "Fit view" (the key F). Menus: File, Edit, View, Geometry, Mesh, Solve, Results, Tools, Help. Selecting in the viewport ¶ A click selects the item under the pointer (8 pixels of tolerance). Ctrl-click adds to or removes from the selection. A click on nothing clears it. A drag longer than 4 pixels selects by a box: curves must lie wholly inside the box, surfaces are chosen by their bounding box, elements by their centre. Changing the selection mode clears the selection. The mouse wheel zooms and the middle button pans. The workflow ¶ The model tree lists the parts of a model in the order you normally fill them in: Tree node What it holds Geometry the geometry operations, in the order they were applied Materials the materials used by the model Regions which material (and thickness and material angle) each surface selection has Mesh mesh settings and the Generate mesh button Initial Condition the starting temperature of a transient analysis Loads & Boundary Conditions fixed temperatures, fluxes, convection, radiation, symmetry, ... Contacts thermal contact between regions Flow streams and networks Enclosures enclosure radiation (not available in this version) Analysis Settings steady or transient, time stepping, output, nonlinear controls Solution the result objects (contour plots, vector plots) after a solve Right-click a node to see its actions. Loads can be added, renamed, duplicated, suppressed and deleted. Materials, streams, contacts and enclosures can be renamed, duplicated and deleted. 1. Geometry ¶ The Geometry menu has Point..., Line..., Arc..., Spline..., Rectangle..., Circle..., Polygon..., Surface from curves..., Union..., Cut..., Intersect..., Translate..., Rotate..., Mirror..., Scale..., Delete..., Import STEP/BREP/DXF..., Snap to grid and Rebuild geometry. Each operation opens a dialog with numeric entry. The geometry is rebuilt by itself after every OK. Notes: For Union, Cut and Intersect select the shapes in the viewport first. The earliest selected shape (in history order) is the object; the others are the tools. The parameters of Translate, Rotate, Mirror and Scale follow the display units: lengths and angles are shown and typed in the display units, and the scale factor is a plain number. An operation that later operations refer to cannot be deleted. If a rebuild fails, the old geometry stays, is marked out of date, and the error is reported. Edit > Undo recovers. DXF import needs the dxf extra ( Installation ). See Limitations for what it ignores. A new model is a planar model. The window has no control to change that. 2. Materials and regions ¶ Right-click Materials and choose Add material. The new material starts as a copy of the first library material, so check every value. Each physical property has a mode box (Constant, Table or Expression) above its value; leave it on Constant for a constant. Tools > Material library... opens the built-in library ( Materials ). Right-click Regions and choose Add region. In its Selection field press "Pick in viewport", set the toolbar to Surface, click the surfaces, press Apply, then press "Pick in viewport" again to switch picking off. Choose the Material, and set the Thickness (planar models) and the Material angle if needed. 3. Loads and boundary conditions ¶ Right-click Loads & Boundary Conditions, choose Add, then one of: Add Fixed Temperature, Add Heat Flux, Add Heat Flow, Add Heat Generation, Add Heat Power, Add Convection, Add Correlation Convection, Add Radiation to Ambient, Add Symmetry, Add Adiabatic. Each load has a Selection field that works as described for regions (set the toolbar to Curve for edges). Selecting a load in the tree highlights its curves, and the viewport shows load symbols. Press Enter after typing a number. The value is applied when you press Enter or leave the field. Each applied change is one undo step. A value may be a Constant, a Table against time, or an Expression of time, position and temperature. Expressions are always evaluated in SI units ( Units ). Heat flows count as positive when they enter the body. Correlation Convection takes its heat-transfer coefficient from a correlation . A correlation used outside its validity range still gives a value and logs one warning. A Contact (right-click Contacts, Add contact) starts with an empty selection and a conductance of 0, which you must set. A temperature-dependent conductance is refused. Streams are under Flow: right-click the node Streams and choose Add stream. The Network node is also under Flow. Results > Flow results... shows the fluid temperature along the stream. Tools > HTC calculator... evaluates a correlation at single values without a model. 4. Mesh ¶ Click the Mesh node. The panel has, among others, "Global element size", "Element order" and "Element shape". Press Generate mesh (or use Mesh > Generate mesh). The status bar reports the number of nodes and elements and the mesh is drawn in the viewport. 5. Analysis settings and initial condition ¶ Click Analysis Settings. "Analysis type" is steady or transient . A transient analysis shows "End time", "Initial time step", "Smallest time step", "Largest time step", "Adaptive time step", "Time-step tolerance", "Largest temperature change per step", "Theta", "Lumped capacitance" and the output controls ("Output steps", "Store every n-th step", "Output times"). The nonlinear controls are "Residual tolerance", "Temperature tolerance", "Maximum iterations" and "Line search". Click Initial Condition for a transient analysis. "Kind" is uniform , expression , per_region or from_results . The initial state (step 0) is always stored. 6. Validate and solve ¶ Solve > Validate checks the model before solving and lists errors and warnings in the Issues dock. Errors must be fixed first. Solve > Solve runs the analysis on its own thread. A window titled "Solving" shows the progress and stays open, with a "Finished" state, so you can read the residual chart. Solve > Cancel solve stops a run. The steps already written are kept. Solve > Continue transient run continues a transient run (see below). The Messages dock shows the log, including the heat entering through each load and the relative imbalance of the energy balance. 7. Results ¶ After a solve the Solution node holds a temperature contour (for example "Temperature 1"). Its panel has "Levels", "Banded (otherwise smooth)", "Colour scale" and "Mesh overlay", and, for a transient run, a "Step" slider and spin box, a "Time" box and "Play". The Results menu has: Add contour, Add vector plot, Probe, Play animation, Nodal history..., Path plot..., Finish path plot, Cancel path plot, Heat-flow history, Energy balance and Flow results.... Nodal history and Path plot ask you to pick nodes or path points in the viewport first. Probe shows x, y and the value at the pixel you click. It is a rough check; use the CSV export for exact values. File > Export has: Viewport image..., Nodal results (CSV)..., ParaView (VTU)... and Animation (GIF).... The CSV has the columns step, time, node, x, y, T, qx, qy in SI units. Charts have their own export. Which things are out of date ¶ An edit makes parts of the work out of date. What is affected depends on what you changed: You changed Out of date the geometry geometry, mesh and results the mesh settings, the model type, or a selection the mesh settings use mesh and results anything else (loads, materials, analysis settings, ...) results only How it shows: Results panels show "These results are out of date: the model changed since the solve." Chart windows are marked "(out of date)" in their title when new results arrive. They are not redrawn. Solve is not available while the geometry or the mesh is out of date. Press Rebuild geometry and Generate mesh first (the status bar says "The mesh is out of date; regenerate it before solving"). Changing the display units ( Units ) makes nothing out of date. Selection tags and the selection named "all" are caches of the build. A rebuild is not an undo step and does not make anything out of date by itself. If you edit the model while a solve is running, the solve uses its own copy. When it finishes, the results are stored but marked out of date. If the mesh or the build was replaced meanwhile, the results are discarded (the file stays on disk). Undo and redo ¶ Edit > Undo and Edit > Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y). Every applied property change, every geometry operation, every change of units and every tree action (add, rename, duplicate, delete) is one undo step. Units ¶ Tools > Units... chooses the units numbers are shown and typed in. The default is SI with temperatures in kelvin. See Units . Press Enter after typing, and remember that 100 degC is 373.15 K when the units are K. Examples ¶ File > Examples opens ready-made models: the verification cases V-01 to V-21, V-27 to V-29, V-32 and V-35 ( Verification ). They are good starting points: open one, look at how it is set up, change it. Files and where results are stored ¶ File > New, Open..., Save, Save As... and Recent files work as usual. The model is a JSON file ( .tfea ). Results are stored in an HDF5 file named after the model with .h5 added: model.tfea.h5 beside model.tfea . A model that was never saved writes its results to a temporary folder. When you open a saved model, its results file is attached again once a mesh exists, so press Generate mesh after opening to see the results. The results file also holds a copy of the model it was solved from. Continuing a transient run ¶ A transient run can be continued from its last stored step to a later end time. The new steps are added to the same results file. Raise "End time" in Analysis Settings. (A run that was cancelled can be continued without raising it.) Choose Solve > Continue transient run . On the command line: thermalfea solve model.tfea --restart . From Python: api.solve(model, mesh, path=..., restart=True) . What to know: The mesh, the materials, thicknesses and material angles of the regions, and the streams must be the same as in the results file, or the restart is refused and the file is left unchanged. So is a steady solution, a last step that did not converge, and an end time the file has already reached. Loads and solver settings may change. The continued steps use the current model, which replaces the model stored in the results file. A load that you changed takes effect from the restart time. With a fixed time step the continued run repeats an uninterrupted run (to round-off in the linear case). With adaptive stepping the controller's history is not stored, so the steps differ from those of an uninterrupted run within the time-stepping tolerance. From the command line ¶ Build and save the model in the window (File > Save) or from a script, then: thermalfea info model.tfea thermalfea solve model.tfea info prints counts and a quality line. solve prints one progress line per step and a text summary, and writes model.tfea.h5 ( Installation has the options and exit codes). Results can then be read by the Python API or opened in the window. From Python ¶ Everything the window does is available from thermalfea.api . This script builds a plate, solves it, prints the summary and saves the model: from thermalfea import api from thermalfea.model.bcs import Convection, FixedTemperature model = api.new_model("planar", name="plate") geo = api.Geometry(model) geo.rectangle(0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 0.1) built = api.build(model) api.select_curves(model, built, name="bottom", where=lambda c: abs(c.center[1]) < 1e-9) api.select_curves(model, built, name="top", where=lambda c: abs(c.center[1] - 0.1) < 1e-9) api.assign_region(model, "all", material="Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6") model.bcs.append(FixedTemperature("base", "bottom", T=373.15)) model.bcs.append(Convection("cooling", "top", h=25.0, T_inf=293.15)) model.mesh_settings.global_size = 0.01 mesh = api.mesh(model, built) results = api.solve(model, mesh, built=built) print(api.summary(results)) api.save(model, "plate.tfea") All values are SI, with temperature in kelvin. Other calls: api.load , api.plot_contour , api.plot_vectors , api.plot_path , api.plot_history , api.export_csv , api.export_vtu , api.export_animation and api.htc . Without path= , api.solve writes the results to a temporary folder; api.results_path(model_path) gives the name beside a model file. Pass built= to api.solve so that the model is validated first.

docs.text: An edit makes parts of the work out of date. What is affected depends on what you changed: You changed Out of date the geometry geometry, mesh and results the mesh settings, the model type, or a selection the mesh settings use mesh and results anything else (loads, materials, analysis settings, ...) results only How it shows: Results panels show "These results are out of date: the model changed since the solve." Chart windows are marked "(out of date)" in their title when new results arrive. They are not redrawn. Solve is not available while the geometry or the mesh is out of date. Press Rebuild geometry and Generate mesh first (the status bar says "The mesh is out of date; regenerate it before solving"). Changing the display units ( Units ) makes nothing out of date. Selection tags and the selection named "all" are caches of the build. A rebuild is not an undo step and does not make anything out of date by itself. If you edit the model while a solve is running, the solve uses its own copy. When it finishes, the results are stored but marked out of date. If the mesh or the build was replaced meanwhile, the results are discarded (the file stays on disk).
docs.title: Which things are out of date

docs.text: Edit > Undo and Edit > Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y). Every applied property change, every geometry operation, every change of units and every tree action (add, rename, duplicate, delete) is one undo step.
docs.title: Undo and redo

docs.text: Tools > Units... chooses the units numbers are shown and typed in. The default is SI with temperatures in kelvin. See Units . Press Enter after typing, and remember that 100 degC is 373.15 K when the units are K.
docs.title: Units

docs.text: File > Examples opens ready-made models: the verification cases V-01 to V-21, V-27 to V-29, V-32 and V-35 ( Verification ). They are good starting points: open one, look at how it is set up, change it.
docs.title: Examples

docs.text: File > New, Open..., Save, Save As... and Recent files work as usual. The model is a JSON file ( .tfea ). Results are stored in an HDF5 file named after the model with .h5 added: model.tfea.h5 beside model.tfea . A model that was never saved writes its results to a temporary folder. When you open a saved model, its results file is attached again once a mesh exists, so press Generate mesh after opening to see the results. The results file also holds a copy of the model it was solved from.
docs.title: Files and where results are stored

docs.text: A transient run can be continued from its last stored step to a later end time. The new steps are added to the same results file. Raise "End time" in Analysis Settings. (A run that was cancelled can be continued without raising it.) Choose Solve > Continue transient run . On the command line: thermalfea solve model.tfea --restart . From Python: api.solve(model, mesh, path=..., restart=True) . What to know: The mesh, the materials, thicknesses and material angles of the regions, and the streams must be the same as in the results file, or the restart is refused and the file is left unchanged. So is a steady solution, a last step that did not converge, and an end time the file has already reached. Loads and solver settings may change. The continued steps use the current model, which replaces the model stored in the results file. A load that you changed takes effect from the restart time. With a fixed time step the continued run repeats an uninterrupted run (to round-off in the linear case). With adaptive stepping the controller's history is not stored, so the steps differ from those of an uninterrupted run within the time-stepping tolerance.
docs.title: Continuing a transient run

docs.text: Build and save the model in the window (File > Save) or from a script, then: thermalfea info model.tfea thermalfea solve model.tfea info prints counts and a quality line. solve prints one progress line per step and a text summary, and writes model.tfea.h5 ( Installation has the options and exit codes). Results can then be read by the Python API or opened in the window.
docs.title: From the command line

docs.text: Everything the window does is available from thermalfea.api . This script builds a plate, solves it, prints the summary and saves the model: from thermalfea import api from thermalfea.model.bcs import Convection, FixedTemperature model = api.new_model("planar", name="plate") geo = api.Geometry(model) geo.rectangle(0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 0.1) built = api.build(model) api.select_curves(model, built, name="bottom", where=lambda c: abs(c.center[1]) < 1e-9) api.select_curves(model, built, name="top", where=lambda c: abs(c.center[1] - 0.1) < 1e-9) api.assign_region(model, "all", material="Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6") model.bcs.append(FixedTemperature("base", "bottom", T=373.15)) model.bcs.append(Convection("cooling", "top", h=25.0, T_inf=293.15)) model.mesh_settings.global_size = 0.01 mesh = api.mesh(model, built) results = api.solve(model, mesh, built=built) print(api.summary(results)) api.save(model, "plate.tfea") All values are SI, with temperature in kelvin. Other calls: api.load , api.plot_contour , api.plot_vectors , api.plot_path , api.plot_history , api.export_csv , api.export_vtu , api.export_animation and api.htc . Without path= , api.solve writes the results to a temporary folder; api.results_path(model_path) gives the name beside a model file. Pass built= to api.solve so that the model is validated first.
docs.title: From Python

docs.text: Installation ¶ ThermalFEA is installed from its source folder into a Python virtual environment. A packaged Windows installer does not exist yet; it is planned (task M11.5). Requirements ¶ Python 3.11 or newer (the project is developed with Python 3.13). The packages the program depends on are installed automatically: NumPy, SciPy, gmsh, PySide6, Matplotlib, h5py, meshio and Pillow. pandas is installed only with the examples extra. Get the source ¶ The source is on GitHub at https://github.com/dilleyrd/thermal-fea . Clone it with Git: git clone https://github.com/dilleyrd/thermal-fea.git cd thermal-fea or download it as a zip file from that page (Code > Download ZIP) and unpack it. Install ¶ From the project folder (the one with pyproject.toml ), create a virtual environment and install the package in it. On Windows, in a terminal: python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e . Use the virtual environment's Python for everything below. Do not install into the system Python. Optional extras ¶ Extra Installs Needed for dxf ezdxf importing DXF files. Without it a DXF import stops with a message that says how to install it. examples pandas running the pump-closure showcase scripts in examples/pump_closure/showcase/ dev pytest , pytest-qt , ruff running the tests and the style check docs mkdocs building this guide Install an extra by naming it in brackets: .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e ".[dxf]" .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e ".[dev,docs]" Start the program ¶ .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m thermalfea.gui.app An installation made since 2026-11-23 also has the command .venv\Scripts\thermalfea-gui.exe , which opens the same window without a console. (An older installation gets it after pip install -e . is run again.) The main window has a model tree ("Model", top left), a property panel ("Properties", below it), the viewport in the middle and a "Messages" dock at the bottom. The next page, Getting started , walks through them. The command line ¶ The installation adds a thermalfea command to the virtual environment (run it as .venv\Scripts\thermalfea.exe , or .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m thermalfea.cli ). thermalfea info model.tfea thermalfea solve model.tfea thermalfea solve model.tfea -o results.h5 thermalfea solve model.tfea --restart thermalfea info model.tfea builds and meshes the model and prints the number of surfaces, curves and points, the materials, regions and loads, the streams, contacts and enclosures, the mesh size and a short quality line. thermalfea solve model.tfea builds, meshes and solves the model. It prints one progress line per step and then a text summary, with a table of the streams when the model has any. The results go to model.tfea.h5 beside the model. -o RESULTS , --output RESULTS writes the results to the file you name instead. --restart continues the transient run stored in the results file, from its last stored step to the end time of the model, and adds the new steps to the same file. See Getting started . -v , --verbose (given before the command name) also shows the informational log messages. Warnings (for example a correlation used outside its validity range) are always shown. Exit codes: Code Meaning 0 success 1 a ThermalFEA error: a bad model, a geometry or mesh failure, a model that fails validation 2 the solution did not converge Called with no command, thermalfea prints its usage and exits with 0. Run the tests ¶ The check script runs the style check and then the whole test suite, and stops at the first failure: .\scripts\check.ps1 Build this guide ¶ The reference pages of the guide are generated from the project's documents and code. From the project folder: .venv\Scripts\python.exe scripts\build_guide.py .venv\Scripts\python.exe -m mkdocs build --strict The first command rewrites the generated pages in guide/ (with --check it only reports whether they are out of date). The second builds the site into site/ .

docs.text: Limitations ¶ Each entry says what is not available or not as you might expect, and, where the project documents give one, what to do instead. Entries come from the plan, the handover notes and the list of open questions ( docs/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md ) of the project. Not in this version ¶ Two dimensions only. There is no 3D analysis and no 3D viewport. No flow simulation. The flow solver is a one-dimensional stream and pipe-network model; it is not CFD (no Navier-Stokes solution). No coupled physics. No structural or thermal-stress coupling and no other physics. No participating-media radiation. No parallel or distributed solving. No packaged Windows installer. Install from source ( Installation ). The installer is planned (task M11.5). Features on hold ¶ The owner has put these on hold. The theory is written down ( Theory , §10 and §12), but the program does not use it. A model that contains an enclosure, or a region whose material has a phase change, is refused by the validation and by the solver with a message that says so; it is never solved with that part left out. Enclosure (surface-to-surface) radiation (milestone M9). The model has an "Enclosures" node and an enclosure class, but no solver module evaluates enclosures, so a model with an enclosure is not solved. Use radiation to ambient where the surroundings can be treated as a single ambient temperature. When it is built, it will come for planar models first; the axisymmetric version (task M9.5) is the hardest task of the plan and may come later. The verification cases V-22a to V-24 are not active. Phase change (latent heat) (task M10.2). A material has a phase-change field in its data, but the solver does not use it; a region with such a material is not solved. The verification case V-36 is not active. HTML report (task M10.5). For a record of a solution use the text summary ( api.summary , or the output of thermalfea solve ), the CSV and ParaView (VTU) exports and the plot exports. Not yet reviewed or checked ¶ The window has not been reviewed by a person. The human gate M8.G (build two verification cases in the window and list every point of friction) is not done. The window tests run without a screen; on 2026-11-23 a scripted session on a real screen (V-10, V-17, V-27 and the dialogs, with screenshots) found and fixed layout and display defects. Expect further findings in usability. Property and correlation sources. Since 2026-11-23 every built-in property comes from Incropera et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer , 7th ed. (2011), Appendix A, except water, which comes from the NIST Chemistry WebBook. Every correlation cites its equation in that book, except the Churchill 1977 friction factor. See Materials and Correlations . One printed value looks like a misprint and is kept as printed: oxygen μ at 1300 K (open question Q30). Not yet done: the verification report (task M11.2), the performance benchmark (M11.3) and the release review (M11.6). Several choices await the owner's confirmation (open questions Q11, Q14, Q18.2, Q20, Q21, Q22, Q23, Q24, Q25). The entries below say which. Modelling ¶ A new model is planar. The window has no control to change a model to axisymmetric (the examples V-05 and V-07 are axisymmetric; from Python, api.new_model takes the type). Free points and curves inside a surface are not part of the mesh. After the geometry is built, points and curves that bound no surface are removed. A point load or a probe line cannot be made this way. The selection named "all" is reserved. Every build recreates it. A mesh node cannot be placed at a given point in the window. To read a value at a point, draw the geometry so that the point is a vertex (the verification cases do this with two rectangles) and read the value from the CSV export. The mesh quality report only measures. It applies no pass or fail threshold. A total heat flow or power, and a fixed temperature, cannot depend on temperature. Use a flux, a convection condition or a time function instead. A total heat flow or power cannot depend on position either (it is spread uniformly); use a heat flux or a heat generation. Material properties may depend on temperature only. A property that uses t, x or y is refused, and so is one that is not finite (for example sqrt(T - 400) below 400 K). An inclined plate is limited to ±90° from vertical. A larger or non-finite angle is refused; use the horizontal-plate correlations for a horizontal face. A steady analysis evaluates time-dependent loads at t = 0. The nonlinear iteration is a modified Newton method. Derivatives of properties and of coefficients with respect to temperature are deliberately left out of the tangent, so strongly nonlinear problems may need more iterations. A solution that does not converge raises an error (command line exit code 2); it is never returned silently. Thermal contact ¶ A temperature-dependent contact conductance is refused. A function of time and position is accepted. Results have duplicated nodes along a contact. The program splits the mesh along the contact when it solves. The original nodes keep their numbers and the new nodes are added at the end, so node numbers picked on the mesh stay valid. Heat crossing a contact is not in the energy balance, because it is internal to the body. The solver computes it (in watts, from the lower to the higher region number), but it is not yet written to the results file or shown in the program. The pump-closure example ( examples/pump_closure ) shows how to compute it from a script. The geometry factor (thickness or 2πr) is taken from the side with the lower region number. Two regions of different thickness meeting at a contact are not treated specially. A fixed temperature on a geometry point at the end of a contact curve fixes one side only (the side of the lower region number). On a curve it fixes each side's own nodes. DXF import ¶ Only LINE, ARC, CIRCLE, LWPOLYLINE (with bulges) and SPLINE entities are used. Other entity types (for example ELLIPSE, old-style POLYLINE, HATCH, INSERT, TEXT) are ignored, with one warning. Chains that do not close are ignored, with a warning. A drawing with no closed outline, a point where more than two segment ends meet, and anything outside the plane z = 0 are errors. Outlines are assumed not to cross each other; crossing outlines are not detected. A closed outline inside an even number of other outlines becomes a surface; one inside an odd number becomes a hole. The units header of the file ( $INSUNITS ) is not read. Give the scale on import, as for STEP and BREP files. End points closer than 1e-6 of the largest extent of the drawing are treated as one point. This tolerance cannot be changed. An arc is split into pieces of at most 120 degrees, so a semicircle becomes two curves. DXF import needs the optional ezdxf package. Units ¶ Expressions are always evaluated in SI, whatever the display units. See Units . These places still show SI only: the HTC calculator window, the solve-progress dialog and the solver messages, the extra parameters of a correlation, the CSV and VTU exports (the chart CSV follows the display units) and the api.summary text. Results are shown in the units of the model stored in the results file until you change the units in the session. A model whose file units differ from those its results were solved with therefore shows the results in the older units until you use Tools > Units... once. Convection and flow ¶ A correlation outside its validity range is still evaluated. One warning is logged for each boundary condition and solve. Check the range on the Correlations page. The automatic characteristic length of a plate or vertical channel is the length of the selection. For horizontal plates it is half of that, the book's area/perimeter of a strip or ring. Cylinders, spheres and non-circular sections need a length. The jets take theirs from the nozzle size. An explicit characteristic length always wins. Internal duct flow is not a convection boundary condition. Use a stream. The Dittus-Boelter and Sieder-Tate options replace Gnielinski for turbulent flow. Their ranges (Re at least 1e4) are not enforced in the transition region, and a stream logs no validity warnings for them; the heat-transfer calculator does. Fluid properties outside the table keep the end values and log one warning for each fluid. For an ideal gas the expansion coefficient is still 1/T. Fluid thermal storage is neglected: the fluid in a stream is quasi-steady. A stream has no initial condition; its starting temperatures follow from the initial wall temperatures. One specific heat per stream, taken at its inlet temperature (open question Q18.2, awaiting confirmation). Flow must run along the path. A stream needs a positive mass flow, and a network solution that drives a stream against its path is refused. Every network branch needs a stream, which supplies its flow area, hydraulic diameter, roughness and fluid. Two duct branches may not name one stream. Through-plane streams are refused in axisymmetric models. Time stepping and restart ¶ The first step uses backward Euler (theta = 1) when the start is out of equilibrium with the loads or the initial temperature differs from a prescribed value. Later jumps are detected only at the start of a step; a jump that falls strictly inside a step is not seen. Restart allows changed loads and settings. The mesh, the region materials, thicknesses and material angles, and the streams must be those of the results file, or the restart is refused. Loads and settings are not compared, and the model stored in the results file is replaced by the current one. Restart with automatic stepping does not reproduce an uninterrupted run exactly: the controller's history is not stored, so the steps differ within the time-stepping tolerance. With a fixed step the runs agree to round-off (linear case) or to the iteration tolerance (nonlinear). A restart is refused for a steady solution, for a last step that did not converge and for an end time the file already reached. Known defects from the code review ¶ A code review on 2026-11-20 ( REVIEW.md in the repository) found nine defects. All nine are fixed: three in restart (see Time stepping and restart ) and six by tasks M11.12–M11.16 on 2026-11-22. A second review, of 2026-11-21 ( REVIEW-2.md ), is being worked through as tasks M11.17–M11.36. The property tables and correlations were rebuilt from the reference text on 2026-11-23 (tasks M11.37–M11.42). The window ¶ Animation export to GIF blocks the window while a long animation is written. Animation export to MP4 needs ffmpeg on the PATH (for example winget install Gyan.FFmpeg ); without it, write a GIF. Probe, chart path pick and the stream "pick path points" toggle all listen to viewport clicks. The probe and the chart path pick exclude each other, but the stream toggle does not switch the others off, and it leaves the selection mode at "None" when turned off. Probe reads the pixel you click, not a coordinate. For exact values use the CSV export. Selections are named after the field that created them ("Convection 1 selection"), and the tree does not offer to rename a selection. Open charts are not redrawn when new results arrive. They are marked "(out of date)".

These places still show SI only: the HTC calculator window, the solve-progress dialog and the solver messages, the extra parameters of a correlation, the CSV and VTU exports (the chart CSV follows the display units) and the api.summary text. Results are shown in the units of the model stored in the results file until you change the units in the session. A model whose file units differ from those its results were solved with therefore shows the results in the older units until you use Tools > Units... once.
docs.title: Units

docs.text: A correlation outside its validity range is still evaluated. One warning is logged for each boundary condition and solve. Check the range on the Correlations page. The automatic characteristic length of a plate or vertical channel is the length of the selection. For horizontal plates it is half of that, the book's area/perimeter of a strip or ring. Cylinders, spheres and non-circular sections need a length. The jets take theirs from the nozzle size. An explicit characteristic length always wins. Internal duct flow is not a convection boundary condition. Use a stream. The Dittus-Boelter and Sieder-Tate options replace Gnielinski for turbulent flow. Their ranges (Re at least 1e4) are not enforced in the transition region, and a stream logs no validity warnings for them; the heat-transfer calculator does. Fluid properties outside the table keep the end values and log one warning for each fluid. For an ideal gas the expansion coefficient is still 1/T. Fluid thermal storage is neglected: the fluid in a stream is quasi-steady. A stream has no initial condition; its starting temperatures follow from the initial wall temperatures. One specific heat per stream, taken at its inlet temperature (open question Q18.2, awaiting confirmation). Flow must run along the path. A stream needs a positive mass flow, and a network solution that drives a stream against its path is refused. Every network branch needs a stream, which supplies its flow area, hydraulic diameter, roughness and fluid. Two duct branches may not name one stream. Through-plane streams are refused in axisymmetric models.
docs.title: Convection and flow

docs.text: The first step uses backward Euler (theta = 1) when the start is out of equilibrium with the loads or the initial temperature differs from a prescribed value. Later jumps are detected only at the start of a step; a jump that falls strictly inside a step is not seen. Restart allows changed loads and settings. The mesh, the region materials, thicknesses and material angles, and the streams must be those of the results file, or the restart is refused. Loads and settings are not compared, and the model stored in the results file is replaced by the current one. Restart with automatic stepping does not reproduce an uninterrupted run exactly: the controller's history is not stored, so the steps differ within the time-stepping tolerance. With a fixed step the runs agree to round-off (linear case) or to the iteration tolerance (nonlinear). A restart is refused for a steady solution, for a last step that did not converge and for an end time the file already reached.
docs.title: Time stepping and restart

docs.text: A code review on 2026-11-20 ( REVIEW.md in the repository) found nine defects. All nine are fixed: three in restart (see Time stepping and restart ) and six by tasks M11.12–M11.16 on 2026-11-22. A second review, of 2026-11-21 ( REVIEW-2.md ), is being worked through as tasks M11.17–M11.36. The property tables and correlations were rebuilt from the reference text on 2026-11-23 (tasks M11.37–M11.42).
docs.title: Known defects from the code review

docs.text: Animation export to GIF blocks the window while a long animation is written. Animation export to MP4 needs ffmpeg on the PATH (for example winget install Gyan.FFmpeg ); without it, write a GIF. Probe, chart path pick and the stream "pick path points" toggle all listen to viewport clicks. The probe and the chart path pick exclude each other, but the stream toggle does not switch the others off, and it leaves the selection mode at "None" when turned off. Probe reads the pixel you click, not a coordinate. For exact values use the CSV export. Selections are named after the field that created them ("Convection 1 selection"), and the tree does not offer to rename a selection. Open charts are not redrawn when new results arrive. They are marked "(out of date)".
docs.title: The window

docs.text: Material library ¶ Generated page This page is generated from src/thermalfea/materials/data/solids.json and fluids.json by scripts/build_guide.py . Do not edit it here: change the source and run the script again. The built-in library holds solids (conductivity, density and specific heat) and fluids (temperature tables of the properties the convection correlations need). Open it in the program with Tools > Material library.... You can add your own solids and fluids; they are stored in %APPDATA%/ThermalFEA/materials.json . Every value comes from Bergman, Lavine, Incropera and DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer , 7th ed., Wiley, 2011, Appendix A, or from the NIST Chemistry WebBook (water). The source of each entry is listed with it. Solids ¶ Every built-in solid has constant properties, quoted at 300 K. Most are isotropic; four are orthotropic and list a second conductivity k2 across the material axis. A material you create yourself may instead use a table against temperature. docs.text: Generated page This page is generated from src/thermalfea/materials/data/solids.json and fluids.json by scripts/build_guide.py . Do not edit it here: change the source and run the script again. The built-in library holds solids (conductivity, density and specific heat) and fluids (temperature tables of the properties the convection correlations need). Open it in the program with Tools > Material library.... You can add your own solids and fluids; they are stored in %APPDATA%/ThermalFEA/materials.json . Every value comes from Bergman, Lavine, Incropera and DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer , 7th ed., Wiley, 2011, Appendix A, or from the NIST Chemistry WebBook (water). The source of each entry is listed with it.

docs.text: Theory reference ¶ Generated page This page is generated from docs/theory.md by scripts/build_guide.py . Do not edit it here: change the source and run the script again. Every equation the code implements. Implement these exactly; do not re-derive. Symbols: T temperature [K], t time [s], k conductivity [W/m·K], ρ density [kg/m³], c specific heat [J/kg·K], Q volumetric heat generation [W/m³], q heat flux [W/m²], h heat-transfer coefficient [W/m²·K], ε emissivity, σ = 5.670374419e-8 W/m²·K⁴. §1 Governing equation and weak form ¶ ρc ∂T/∂t = ∇·(D ∇T) + Q in the domain, with D the 2×2 conductivity matrix. Boundary conditions on the boundary Γ (n = outward normal, q_n = −n·D∇T = heat leaving): Fixed temperature: T = T̄ Heat flux into the body: −q_n = q̄ Convection: q_n = h (T − T∞) Radiation to ambient: q_n = ε σ (T⁴ − T∞⁴) Discretised with T ≈ N(ξ,η)·T_e the semi-discrete system is C Ṫ + K T = F All integrals carry the geometry factor g : planar: g = thickness of the region [m] (default 1) axisymmetric: g = 2π r, with r = the x coordinate at the integration point so that every assembled force term is in watts. §2 Element matrices ¶ For each element, with B = the 2×n matrix of ∂N/∂x, ∂N/∂y and |J| the Jacobian determinant: Conduction: K_e = Σ_gp Bᵀ D B · g · |J| · w Capacitance: C_e = Σ_gp ρc · NᵀN · g · |J| · w Heat generation: F_e = Σ_gp Q · Nᵀ · g · |J| · w Orthotropic D with principal conductivities k1, k2 and material angle θ (radians, counter-clockwise from x): D = R diag(k1, k2) Rᵀ, R = [[cosθ, −sinθ],[sinθ, cosθ]]. Isotropic: D = k I. Temperature-dependent properties are evaluated at each integration point from the interpolated temperature N·T_e.
