The fluids here do not change phase. §9 Flow solver ¶ §9.1 Stream (fluid temperature along a wall) ¶ A stream is a 1D fluid path with mass flow ṁ [kg/s], inlet temperature T_in, flow area A, wetted perimeter P_wet (for D_h), fluid, and one or more wall boundary sets that it cools or heats. The stream is divided into N cells along its path coordinate s. Fluid node 0 is the inlet (prescribed T_in); fluid node j is the outlet of cell j−1. Fluid nodes are extra DOFs appended after the mesh nodes. Each wall edge element i belongs to the cell containing the s-coordinate of its midpoint (s = projection of the midpoint onto the stream path polyline). Per edge element: conductance G_i = h_i · ∫ g ds over the edge (h from §8.1 using the cell's upstream fluid-node temperature for properties, lagged) wall temperature T_w,i = Σ_j w_j T_j with w_j = ∫ N_j g ds / ∫ g ds Per cell with upstream fluid node u and downstream node d: G = Σ G_i, T̄_w = Σ G_i T_w,i / G, NTU = G /(ṁ c_p) φ = (1 − e^(−NTU)) / NTU (φ = 1 when NTU < 1e-8) Effective fluid temperature seen by the wall: T_f* = (1 − φ) T̄_w + φ T_u Heat from wall edge i to fluid: Q_i = G_i (T_w,i − T_f*) Fluid energy equation: ṁ c_p (T_d − T_u) − Σ_i Q_i = 0 Q_i is removed from the wall nodes of edge i with the same weights w_j. This scheme is exact for a constant wall temperature per cell, cannot oscillate for any NTU, and conserves energy exactly. The resulting matrix rows are linear in the unknown temperatures (for frozen h and c_p) and unsymmetric . Fluid thermal storage is neglected (quasi-steady fluid) — state this in the user guide. Matrix contributions for one cell, written as a conductance-type matrix K_s such that the heat leaving each DOF is K_s·T: for wall DOF a (weight w_a,i on edge i): row a gets Σ_i w_a,i G_i (T_w,i − (1−φ) T̄_w − φ T_u), and row d gets ṁ c_p (T_d − T_u) − Σ_i G_i (T_w,i − (1−φ) T̄_w − φ T_u). Expand T_w,i and T̄_w into nodal weights to obtain the coefficients. Implement this by building the small dense cell matrix with NumPy and scattering it. A stream may also be through-plane (planar models: flow perpendicular to the model plane, such as a cooling hole seen in cross-section). Then the fluid temperature is uniform on the boundary set and equals the specified bulk temperature; the stream only supplies h from §8.1. No fluid DOFs are created. §9.2 Network (flow distribution) ¶ Nodes carry pressure; branches are ducts (§8.1 pressure drop), minor-loss elements, or fixed-flow sources. Boundary conditions: prescribed pressure at a node, or prescribed mass flow into a node. Unknowns: nodal pressures. Branch law: ṁ = sign(Δp) · A √( 2 ρ |Δp| / (f L/D_h + K_minor) ). Linearise as ṁ = c (p_i − p_j) with c = ṁ/Δp from the previous iterate (start with laminar f = 64/Re assumption at Re = 1000). Iterate: assemble Σ c (p_i − p_j) = source at each node, solve, update ṁ and f, under-relax c with factor 0.5, until the largest relative change in any ṁ < 1e-6 (max 200 iterations). Each branch's ṁ then feeds the stream attached to it. Fluid properties in the network use each branch's mean stream temperature; the hydraulic and thermal solutions are alternated inside the nonlinear loop (hydraulics updated at most once per nonlinear iteration, and only when a branch's mean temperature has changed by more than 1 K). §10 Enclosure radiation (grey, diffuse) ¶ Not available in this version Enclosure radiation (surface-to-surface radiation, §10 to §10.2) is not implemented in this version (milestone M9 is on hold). The theory is kept here for completeness; no solver module uses it yet. Faces = boundary edge elements of the enclosure, i = 1…n, length-based area A_i = ∫ g ds, emissivity ε_i, face temperature T_i = Σ w_j T_j (weights as in §9.1), E_b,i = σ T_i⁴. View-factor matrix F (n×n). Open enclosures: F_i∞ = 1 − Σ_j F_ij radiates to a black ambient at T_∞. With E = diag(ε): solve (I − (I − E) F) J = E·E_b + (I − E) F_∞ σT_∞⁴ for radiosity J. Net flux leaving face i: q_i = J_i − Σ_j F_ij J_j − F_i∞ σ T_∞⁴. Precompute once per mesh: M = (I − F)(I − (I−E)F)⁻¹ E and the ambient vector. Then q = M E_b + q_∞, heat Q_i = A_i q_i, distributed to the face's nodes with weights w_j. Residual contribution: −Q. Tangent: ∂Q_i/∂T_j = A_i M_ij 4σT_j³ (dense block; insert it fully when n ≤ 3000, otherwise only its diagonal). §10.1 View factors, planar ¶ For two straight segments i (endpoints a1,a2) and j (endpoints b1,b2) that fully see each other (Hottel crossed strings): F_ij = [ |a1b2| + |a2b1| − |a1b1| − |a2b2| ] / (2 L_i) (use the absolute value; "crossed" strings are the two that intersect) Visibility: a pair is facing if each midpoint lies on the outward-normal side of the other. A pair is fully visible if facing and none of the four end-to-end sight lines intersects any other enclosure segment. If facing but not fully visible, subdivide both segments into m = 8 sub-segments, apply crossed strings to each fully visible sub-pair (testing sight lines between sub-segment endpoints), and sum: F_ij = Σ_sub L_sub,i F_sub / L_i. Use a uniform grid or shapely.STRtree -free hand-written segment-intersection test vectorised with NumPy. Afterwards enforce reciprocity (A_i F_ij ← ½(A_i F_ij + A_j F_ji)) and, for closed enclosures, scale rows so Σ_j F_ij = 1 (repeat both steps 5 times). §10.2 View factors, axisymmetric (task M9.5) ¶ Each face is a conical ring. Compute F_ij by numerical integration of the 3D kernel cosθ_i cosθ_j /(π r²) over the azimuth of ring j (and sub-divisions of both generators), with blockage tested by intersecting each ray with every other ring's cone frustum. Validate against concentric-cylinder and coaxial-disk closed forms (V-22). §11 Thermal contact resistance ¶ Along an interface curve the mesh has duplicated nodes (one set per side). For each pair of matching edge elements with contact conductance h_c [W/m²·K] add, over the 2n interface DOFs [side A; side B]: K_c = Σ_gp h_c g |J_s| w · [[NᵀN, −NᵀN], [−NᵀN, NᵀN]] §12 Phase change (apparent heat capacity) ¶ Not available in this version Phase change (apparent heat capacity) is not implemented in this version (task M10.2 is on hold). The theory is kept here for completeness; no solver module uses it yet. Latent heat L released between T_sol and T_liq is modelled by replacing ρc with ρc + ρL/(T_liq − T_sol) for T_sol ≤ T ≤ T_liq. Require T_liq − T_sol ≥ 1 K, force lumped capacitance and backward Euler, and limit max_dT_per_step to (T_liq − T_sol)/2.
docs.title: Theory

docs.text: Generated page This page is generated from docs/theory.md by scripts/build_guide.py . Do not edit it here: change the source and run the script again. Every equation the code implements. Implement these exactly; do not re-derive. Symbols: T temperature [K], t time [s], k conductivity [W/m·K], ρ density [kg/m³], c specific heat [J/kg·K], Q volumetric heat generation [W/m³], q heat flux [W/m²], h heat-transfer coefficient [W/m²·K], ε emissivity, σ = 5.670374419e-8 W/m²·K⁴.
docs.title: Theory reference

docs.text: ρc ∂T/∂t = ∇·(D ∇T) + Q in the domain, with D the 2×2 conductivity matrix. Boundary conditions on the boundary Γ (n = outward normal, q_n = −n·D∇T = heat leaving): Fixed temperature: T = T̄ Heat flux into the body: −q_n = q̄ Convection: q_n = h (T − T∞) Radiation to ambient: q_n = ε σ (T⁴ − T∞⁴) Discretised with T ≈ N(ξ,η)·T_e the semi-discrete system is C Ṫ + K T = F All integrals carry the geometry factor g : planar: g = thickness of the region [m] (default 1) axisymmetric: g = 2π r, with r = the x coordinate at the integration point so that every assembled force term is in watts.
docs.title: §1 Governing equation and weak form

docs.text: For each element, with B = the 2×n matrix of ∂N/∂x, ∂N/∂y and |J| the Jacobian determinant: Conduction: K_e = Σ_gp Bᵀ D B · g · |J| · w Capacitance: C_e = Σ_gp ρc · NᵀN · g · |J| · w Heat generation: F_e = Σ_gp Q · Nᵀ · g · |J| · w Orthotropic D with principal conductivities k1, k2 and material angle θ (radians, counter-clockwise from x): D = R diag(k1, k2) Rᵀ, R = [[cosθ, −sinθ],[sinθ, cosθ]]. Isotropic: D = k I. Temperature-dependent properties are evaluated at each integration point from the interpolated temperature N·T_e.
docs.title: §2 Element matrices

docs.text: For an edge with shape functions N (1D), |J_s| = ds/dξ: Flux: F_e = Σ_gp q̄ · Nᵀ · g · |J_s| · w Convection: K_e = Σ_gp h · NᵀN · g · |J_s| · w ; F_e = Σ_gp h T∞ · Nᵀ · g · |J_s| · w Total heat flow P [W] applied to a boundary set: convert to uniform flux q̄ = P / A, where A = Σ over the set of ∫ g ds. Total power P [W] applied to a region: Q = P / V, V = ∫ g dA.
docs.title: Boundary (edge) element terms

docs.text: Node ordering is gmsh ordering : corners counter-clockwise, then mid-side nodes in the order (0-1, 1-2, 2-0) for triangles and (0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 3-0) for quads. T3 (ξ,η ∈ unit triangle): N = [1−ξ−η, ξ, η] T6 with L1 = 1−ξ−η, L2 = ξ, L3 = η: N = [L1(2L1−1), L2(2L2−1), L3(2L3−1), 4L1L2, 4L2L3, 4L3L1] Q4 (ξ,η ∈ [−1,1]), corner signs (ξi,ηi) = (−1,−1),(1,−1),(1,1),(−1,1): N_i = ¼(1+ξξi)(1+ηηi) Q8 (serendipity): corners N_i = ¼(1+ξξi)(1+ηηi)(ξξi+ηηi−1); mid-sides with ξi = 0: N_i = ½(1−ξ²)(1+ηηi); with ηi = 0: N_i = ½(1+ξξi)(1−η²). Mid-side positions: (0,−1),(1,0),(0,1),(−1,0). L2 edge (ξ ∈ [−1,1]): N = [½(1−ξ), ½(1+ξ)] L3 edge, gmsh order (end, end, middle): N = [½ξ(ξ−1), ½ξ(ξ+1), 1−ξ²] Quadrature (weights sum to the reference area: ½ for triangles, 4 for quads, 2 for lines): Element Rule T3 3-point: (1/6,1/6), (2/3,1/6), (1/6,2/3), each w = 1/6 T6 6-point degree-4 rule (Dunavant) Q4 2×2 Gauss Q8 3×3 Gauss L2 2-point Gauss L3 3-point Gauss Dunavant degree 4, in area coordinates, weights given for reference area ½: a = 0.445948490915965, b = 0.108103018168070, w = 0.223381589678011 / 2; points (a,a),(a,b),(b,a) as (ξ,η) a = 0.091576213509771, b = 0.816847572980459, w = 0.109951743655322 / 2; points (a,a),(a,b),(b,a) Use the same rule for K, C and F of an element type (keeps the code simple and is exact or better for all terms on straight-sided elements).
docs.title: §3 Shape functions and quadrature

docs.text: T3, Q4: row-sum, C_ii = Σ_j C_ij. T6, Q8: HRZ lumping, C_ii = C_ii(consistent) · (Σ_ij C_ij) / (Σ_k C_kk). Never use row-sum for quadratic elements (gives zero or negative corner terms).
docs.title: Lumped capacitance (option)

docs.text: Partition DOFs into free (f) and prescribed (p). Solve K_ff T_f = F_f − K_fp T̄_p. Never use the penalty method. Reaction heat flow at prescribed nodes (positive = heat entering the body through the constraint) for the transient system: R_p = (C Ṫ + K T − F)_p
docs.title: §4 Fixed temperatures

docs.text: Residual at free DOFs: r(T) = F(T) − K(T) T (K includes convection and radiation tangent-free parts; F includes all load vectors). Radiation to ambient contributes to r r_rad = −Σ_gp ε σ ((N·T)⁴ − T∞⁴) Nᵀ g |J_s| w and to the tangent K_rad = Σ_gp 4 ε σ (N·T)³ NᵀN g |J_s| w Iteration (modified Newton — property derivatives dk/dT, dh/dT are deliberately omitted from the tangent): Assemble K(Tⁱ), F(Tⁱ), K_rad(Tⁱ), r(Tⁱ) with properties and coefficients at Tⁱ. Solve (K + K_rad)_ff ΔT_f = r_f. Line search: s = 1; while ‖r(Tⁱ + sΔT)‖ > (1 − 1e-4·s)‖r(Tⁱ)‖ and s > 1/32: s ← s/2. Tⁱ⁺¹ = Tⁱ + sΔT. Converged when ‖r_f‖₂ ≤ rtol · F_ref and ‖sΔT‖∞ ≤ ttol. F_ref = max(‖F‖₂, ‖K T‖₂, 1e-12). Defaults rtol = 1e-6, ttol = 1e-4 K, max 30 iterations. Round-off floor: the residual test also passes when ‖r_f‖₂ ≤ N ε (‖(|K| |T|)_f‖₂ + ‖F_f‖₂ + ‖r_extra,f‖₂), with N = 100 and ε the machine precision (2.2e-16); ‖sΔT‖∞ ≤ ttol is still required. |K| and |T| are the element-wise absolute values, the subscript f keeps the free rows, and r_extra is the part of r that is not F − K T (for example r_rad). At equilibrium F and K T cancel and F_ref falls to round-off; the floor then accepts a residual at the round-off level of the sums that form it (owner, Q29.1 D1). Not converged after the limit → raise ConvergenceError (steady) or cut the step (transient). A problem is linear when no property, coefficient or load depends on T and there is no radiation. Detect this once; a linear problem takes exactly one solve with no iteration. If any temperature becomes ≤ 0 K during iteration, treat the iteration as failed (halve the line-search step; if that fails, raise).
docs.title: §5 Nonlinear steady solution

docs.text: With g(T, t) = F(T, t) − K(T) T − (radiation term) the "heat-flow imbalance", the step from t_n to t_{n+1} = t_n + Δt solves for T_{n+1}: R(T_{n+1}) = C(T_θ) (T_{n+1} − T_n)/Δt − θ g(T_{n+1}, t_{n+1}) − (1−θ) g(T_n, t_n) = 0 with T_θ = θ T_{n+1} + (1−θ) T_n used only to evaluate ρc. Tangent: A = C/Δt + θ (K + K_rad) evaluated at the current iterate. Newton update: A_ff ΔT_f = −R_f. Line search and convergence test as in §5, with F_ref = max(‖C(T_{n+1}−T_n)/Δt‖₂, ‖F‖₂, ‖K T‖₂, 1e-12). The round-off floor of §5 applies unchanged, with K, F and r_extra assembled at the iterate T_{n+1}. θ = 1 backward Euler ( default ; unconditionally stable, no oscillation) θ = 2/3 Galerkin θ = 1/2 Crank–Nicolson (second order; may oscillate after a thermal shock) g(T_n, t_n) is stored from the end of the previous step, not recomputed. At a step where a prescribed temperature or a load jumps discontinuously, use θ = 1 for that one step. Prescribed temperatures: set T_{n+1,p} = T̄(t_{n+1}) before the first iteration. Linear case: A is constant while Δt is constant — factorise once and reuse ( splu object cached, keyed on Δt).
docs.title: §6 Transient solution (θ-method)

docs.text: After a converged step compute the predictor T_pred = T_n + (Δt/Δt_prev)(T_n − T_{n−1}) (for the first step skip the error test) and the error e = ‖T_{n+1} − T_pred‖∞ / max(T_range, 1 K), T_range = max(T) − min(T) over the model If e > 4·tol: reject the step, Δt ← Δt/2, redo. Otherwise accept and set Δt_next = Δt · clip(0.9 √(tol/e), 0.5, 2.0). Default tol = 0.02. Clamp to [Δt_min, Δt_max]. Newton failure: Δt ← Δt/4, redo. If Δt < Δt_min: raise ConvergenceError . Always shorten a step so that it lands exactly on the next mandatory time : every requested output time, every breakpoint of every load table, and the end time. Also limit the step so the largest nodal change ≤ max_dT_per_step if the user set it. Suggested initial step (shown in the GUI): Δt₀ = h_min² / (4 α_max), α = k/(ρc), h_min = smallest element edge length. Oscillation warning: if consistent capacitance is used and Δt < h² ρc /(6k) for more than 5% of elements, log a warning recommending lumped capacitance or a finer mesh.
docs.title: §6.1 Automatic time stepping

docs.text: Gradient at any element point: ∇T = B T_e. Flux q = −D ∇T. Nodal flux: evaluate q at each element's own nodes (B at the node's local coordinates), then average the contributions of all elements sharing the node that belong to the same region . A node on a material interface therefore has one flux value per region. Element flux: value at the element centroid. Heat flow through a boundary set [W] (positive out of the body): convection set: Σ_gp h (T − T∞) g |J_s| w radiation set: Σ_gp εσ(T⁴ − T∞⁴) g |J_s| w flux set: −Σ_gp q̄ g |J_s| w fixed-temperature set: −Σ R_p over its nodes (§4) Stored energy rate: Ė = Σ (C Ṫ), with Ṫ = (T_{n+1} − T_n)/Δt. Energy balance: (generation + heat in through all boundaries) − Ė = imbalance. Report imbalance / max(|terms|).
docs.title: §7 Recovered quantities

docs.text: Source of every correlation in §8 and §8.1, unless a row names another: [I] Bergman, Lavine, Incropera and DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer , 7th ed., Wiley, 2011. The equation numbers below are the book's (owner's decision, 2026-11-23). h = Nu · k_f / L_c. Fluid properties at the film temperature T_film = (T_s + T∞)/2 unless the correlation states otherwise. T_s is the wall temperature of the previous nonlinear iteration (lagged), either local (at each integration point; default) or the area average over the boundary set (option). Re = ρ V L/μ, Pr = μ c_p/k_f, Ra = g β |T_s − T∞| L³ Pr ρ²/μ², g = 9.80665 m/s². For ideal gases β = 1/T_film; for liquids β comes from the property table. ID Situation Formula L_c Validity [I] plate_forced_avg Flat plate, parallel flow, average Re ≤ 5e5: Nu = 0.664 Re^½ Pr^⅓; else Nu = (0.037 Re^0.8 − 871) Pr^⅓ plate length Pr ≥ 0.6; when Re > 5e5 also Pr ≤ 60 and Re ≤ 1e8 7.30, 7.38 plate_forced_local Flat plate, local at distance x from leading edge Re_x ≤ 5e5: Nu_x = 0.332 Re_x^½ Pr^⅓; else Nu_x = 0.0296 Re_x^0.8 Pr^⅓ x Pr ≥ 0.6; when Re_x > 5e5 also Pr ≤ 60 and Re_x ≤ 1e8 7.23, 7.36 cylinder_crossflow Cylinder in cross flow (Churchill–Bernstein) Nu = 0.3 + 0.62 Re^½ Pr^⅓ [1+(0.4/Pr)^⅔]^(−¼) [1+(Re/282000)^⅝]^(⅘) diameter Re·Pr ≥ 0.2 7.54 square_corner_crossflow Square cylinder, a corner facing the flow, gas Nu = 0.304 Re^0.59 Pr^⅓ D = diagonal (width across the flow) 6000 ≤ Re ≤ 60000 7.52, Table 7.3 square_face_crossflow Square cylinder, a face facing the flow, gas Nu = 0.158 Re^0.66 Pr^⅓ D = side 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 60000 7.52, Table 7.3 hexagon_face_crossflow Hexagonal cylinder, a face facing the flow, gas Re ≤ 20400: Nu = 0.164 Re^0.638 Pr^⅓; else Nu = 0.039 Re^0.78 Pr^⅓ D = corner-to-corner width across the flow 5200 ≤ Re ≤ 105000 7.52, Table 7.3 hexagon_corner_crossflow Hexagonal cylinder, a corner facing the flow, gas Nu = 0.150 Re^0.638 Pr^⅓ D = face-to-face width across the flow 4500 ≤ Re ≤ 90700 7.52, Table 7.3 plate_front_crossflow Thin plate across the flow, upstream face, gas Nu = 0.667 Re^0.500 Pr^⅓ D = plate height across the flow 10000 ≤ Re ≤ 50000 7.52, Table 7.3 plate_back_crossflow Thin plate across the flow, downstream face, gas Nu = 0.191 Re^0.667 Pr^⅓ D = plate height across the flow 7000 ≤ Re ≤ 80000 7.52, Table 7.3 sphere_forced Sphere in a free stream (Whitaker) Nu = 2 + (0.4 Re^½ + 0.06 Re^⅔) Pr^0.4 (μ/μ_s)^¼. All properties at T∞ , except μ_s at T_s diameter 0.71 ≤ Pr ≤ 380, 3.5 ≤ Re ≤ 7.6e4, 1.0 ≤ μ/μ_s ≤ 3.2 7.56 slot_jet Single slot nozzle impinging on the surface, average over |x| ≤ x_r from the jet's centre line (Martin) Nu / Pr^0.42 = 3.06 / (0.5/A_r + H/W + 2.78) · Re^m, m = 0.695 − [1/(4 A_r) + (H/(2W))^1.33 + 3.06]^(−1), A_r = W/(2 x_r); Re = V 2W/ν with V the jet exit velocity 2W 3000 ≤ Re ≤ 9e4, 2 ≤ H/W ≤ 10, 0.025 ≤ A_r ≤ 0.125 7.75, 7.76 round_jet Single round nozzle impinging on the surface, average over r ≤ r_r from the jet's axis (Martin) Nu / Pr^0.42 = G · 2 Re^½ (1 + 0.005 Re^0.55)^½, G = 2 A_r^½ (1 − 2.2 A_r^½) / (1 + 0.2 (H/D − 6) A_r^½), A_r = D²/(4 r_r²); Re = V D/ν with V the jet exit velocity D (nozzle) 2000 ≤ Re ≤ 4e5, 2 ≤ H/D ≤ 12, 0.004 ≤ A_r ≤ 0.04 7.71, 7.72 duct_internal Internal flow, circular or by hydraulic diameter see §8.1 D_h vplate_natural Vertical plate (Churchill–Chu) Nu = {0.825 + 0.387 Ra^(1/6) / [1+(0.492/Pr)^(9/16)]^(8/27)}² height all Ra 9.26 vplate_natural_laminar Vertical plate, laminar (Churchill–Chu; slightly more accurate than 9.26 for Ra ≤ 1e9) Nu = 0.68 + 0.670 Ra^¼ / [1+(0.492/Pr)^(9/16)]^(4/9) height Ra ≤ 1e9 9.27 inclined_natural Plate inclined θ from vertical: the top face of a cold plate or the bottom face of a hot plate as vplate_natural with g → g cos θ length 0 ≤ θ ≤ 60°; for the other face [I] makes no recommendation (see below) 9.26, §9.6.2 hplate_up_natural Horizontal, hot face up or cold face down Ra ≤ 1e7: Nu = 0.54 Ra^¼; else Nu = 0.15 Ra^⅓ area/perimeter 1e4 ≤ Ra ≤ 1e11; when Ra ≤ 1e7 also Pr ≥ 0.7 9.30, 9.31 hplate_down_natural Horizontal, hot face down or cold face up Nu = 0.52 Ra^(1/5) area/perimeter 1e4 ≤ Ra ≤ 1e9, Pr ≥ 0.7 9.32 hcyl_natural Horizontal cylinder (Churchill–Chu) Nu = {0.60 + 0.387 Ra^(1/6) / [1+(0.559/Pr)^(9/16)]^(8/27)}² diameter Ra ≤ 1e12 9.34 sphere_natural Sphere (Churchill) Nu = 2 + 0.589 Ra^¼ / [1+(0.469/Pr)^(9/16)]^(4/9) diameter Pr ≥ 0.7, Ra ≤ 1e11 9.35 vchannel_natural Vertical channel between two parallel isothermal plates, both at T_s (Bar-Cohen–Rohsenow) Nu_S = [576/(Ra_S S/L)² + 2.87/(Ra_S S/L)^½]^(−½), Ra_S = Ra with L → S; h = Nu_S k_f / S S (plate spacing); L = channel height none stated 9.45, Table 9.3 vchannel_one_side_natural Vertical channel, this plate at T_s, the opposite plate adiabatic (Bar-Cohen–Rohsenow) Nu_S = [144/(Ra_S S/L)² + 2.87/(Ra_S S/L)^½]^(−½), Ra_S and h as above S; L = channel height none stated 9.45, Table 9.3 power_law User form h = C · |T_s − T∞|ⁿ — — — For the horizontal-plate pair, pick "up" or "down" automatically at run time from the sign of (T_s − T∞) and the declared face direction. Outside a validity range: still evaluate, and emit one warning per boundary condition per solve. plate_forced_local needs the leading-edge point and flow direction; x is the distance of the integration point from the leading edge along the flow direction (minimum x = 1e-6 m). inclined_natural : when the face direction is declared, a face for which [I] makes no recommendation counts as outside the validity range: the top face ( up ) of a hot plate (T_s > T∞), or the bottom face ( down ) of a cold plate. When no face direction is declared, this is not checked. Characteristic lengths in a 2D model. Horizontal plates. [I] defines L = A_s/P (Eq. 9.29). In a planar model a horizontal face is a strip of unit depth, so A_s/P is half the strip's width; [I] Example 9.3 uses w/2 in the same way. In an axisymmetric model, a horizontal ring from r_i to r_o gives A_s/P = (r_o − r_i)/2. Either way, the automatic L_c of hplate_up_natural and hplate_down_natural is half the total length of the selection . This settles Q17.2. Other correlations. For the other plate correlations and the vertical channels (channel height), the automatic L_c is the total length of the selection. Diameters. The cylinder, sphere and non-circular cylinder correlations need L_c (the diameter or D) given. An explicit L_c always overrides the automatic one. Extra inputs (Data §8 params ): Vertical channels: S , the plate spacing [m]. slot_jet : W , the slot width [m]; H , the nozzle-to-surface distance [m]; x_r , the half-width of the region averaged over [m]. The default x_r is half the total length of the selection. round_jet : D , the nozzle diameter [m]; H [m]; r_r , the radius of the region averaged over [m]. In an axisymmetric model the default r_r is the largest radial coordinate of the selection; a planar model must give r_r . The jets take their L_c from these inputs , so a given L_c is refused.
docs.title: §8 Convection from correlations

docs.text: Re = ṁ D_h /(A μ), D_h = 4A/P_wet. Properties at the bulk fluid temperature. Laminar (Re ≤ 2300): Nu_lam from the tables below ([I] Tables 8.1 and 8.2). Turbulent (Re ≥ 4000): Gnielinski ([I] 8.62, with f from 8.21) Nu = (f/8)(Re − 1000) Pr / [1 + 12.7 (f/8)^½ (Pr^⅔ − 1)], f = (0.790 ln Re − 1.64)⁻² (valid 0.5 ≤ Pr ≤ 2000, 3000 ≤ Re ≤ 5e6). Transition (2300 < Re < 4000): linear interpolation in Re between Nu_lam and Nu_Gnielinski(Re = 4000). [I] gives no transition correlation; this rule is the program's. Cross-section ( cross_section ) Nu_lam, constant wall T Nu_lam, constant flux Circular ( circular ) 3.66 4.36 Parallel plates, both heated ( parallel_plates ) 7.54 8.23 Parallel plates, one side insulated ( parallel_plates_one_side ) 4.86 5.39 Square ( square ) 2.98 3.61 Rectangle, sides b/a = 1.43 ( rectangle_1_43 ) 3.08 3.73 Rectangle, b/a = 2.0 ( rectangle_2 ) 3.39 4.12 Rectangle, b/a = 3.0 ( rectangle_3 ) 3.96 4.79 Rectangle, b/a = 4.0 ( rectangle_4 ) 4.44 5.33 Rectangle, b/a = 8.0 ( rectangle_8 ) 5.60 6.49 Triangle ( triangle ) 2.49 3.11 Concentric annulus , one surface at constant temperature and the other insulated ([I] Table 8.2). D_h = D_o − D_i. The stream gives diameter_ratio = D_i/D_o. Nu is linearly interpolated in D_i/D_o between the rows; the program, not [I], sets that rule. D_i/D_o Nu_i: inner surface heated ( annulus_inner ) Nu_o: outer surface heated ( annulus_outer ) 0 — 3.66 0.05 17.46 4.06 0.10 11.56 4.11 0.25 7.37 4.23 0.50 5.74 4.43 1.00 4.86 4.86 annulus_inner needs 0.05 ≤ D_i/D_o ≤ 1. annulus_outer needs 0 ≤ D_i/D_o ≤ 1. [I] gives only constant-temperature values for the annulus, so a constant-flux request is refused. Default is the constant-wall-temperature value. Optional user selections, each replacing Gnielinski as the turbulent formula (the laminar value and the transition rule are kept): Dittus–Boelter ([I] 8.60): Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^n. n = 0.4 if the wall is hotter than the fluid, else 0.3. Valid for 0.6 ≤ Pr ≤ 160 and Re ≥ 1e4. Sieder–Tate ([I] 8.61): Nu = 0.027 Re^(4/5) Pr^(1/3) (μ/μ_s)^0.14. μ_s is taken at the cell's mean wall temperature T̄_w; the other properties at the bulk temperature. Valid for 0.7 ≤ Pr ≤ 16700 and Re ≥ 1e4. [I] recommends it for flows with large property variation, such as oils. Friction factor, all regimes (Churchill 1977, not in [I]), roughness e: f = 8 [ (8/Re)¹² + (A + B)^(−1.5) ]^(1/12), A = [2.457 ln( 1 / ((7/Re)^0.9 + 0.27 e/D_h) )]¹⁶, B = (37530/Re)¹⁶ Pressure drop of a duct of length L with minor-loss coefficient K_minor: Δp = (f L/D_h + K_minor) · ρ V²/2, V = ṁ/(ρ A).
docs.title: §8.1 Internal duct flow

docs.text: Recorded so that no task adds them without a decision. On 2026-11-23 the owner judged the correlations in use adequate and declined the enclosure, mixed-convection and Table 8.1 f·Re additions (Q30.4): Circular cylinder, Hilpert ([I] 7.52, Table 7.2) and Zukauskas (7.53). These cover the same case as Churchill–Bernstein (7.54), which is kept. Horizontal cylinder, Morgan (9.33, Table 9.1) is not used either; Churchill–Chu (9.34) is kept. Liquid-metal forms : the flat plate (7.32) and fully developed tube flow (8.64, 8.65). Mercury is the only liquid metal built in. Other correlations used outside their Pr range warn as usual. Flat plate with uniform surface flux (7.45–7.48) or an unheated starting length (7.60–7.64). The surface conditions these assume are not known to a load. Tube banks (7.58, 7.59), packed beds (7.81), falling drops (7.57), and arrays of jets (7.73, 7.77). These need array geometry and a mean fluid temperature that a single-surface load does not have. Laminar entry lengths (8.57, 8.58). These give a Nusselt number averaged from the inlet to x, but the stream needs a local value in each cell. Colebrook friction (8.20) and laminar f·Re of non-circular sections (Table 8.1). Churchill 1977 is kept; it applies to circular ducts and to D_h. Using Table 8.1's f·Re would need a rule for joining it to the turbulent branch, which [I] does not give (OPEN_QUESTIONS Q30). Isoflux vertical channels (9.46), inclined channels (9.47), and the isolated-plate optimum spacings (Table 9.3). The isothermal form 9.45 is used. Enclosures: rectangular cavities, concentric cylinders and spheres (9.49–9.63). They couple two surfaces across a cavity, and a convection load sees only one ambient temperature (Q30). Mixed free and forced convection (9.64). This needs two correlations in one load (Q30). Boiling and condensation (chapter 10). The fluids here do not change phase.
docs.title: §8.2 Correlations of [I] that are not used

docs.text: A stream is a 1D fluid path with mass flow ṁ [kg/s], inlet temperature T_in, flow area A, wetted perimeter P_wet (for D_h), fluid, and one or more wall boundary sets that it cools or heats. The stream is divided into N cells along its path coordinate s. Fluid node 0 is the inlet (prescribed T_in); fluid node j is the outlet of cell j−1. Fluid nodes are extra DOFs appended after the mesh nodes. Each wall edge element i belongs to the cell containing the s-coordinate of its midpoint (s = projection of the midpoint onto the stream path polyline). Per edge element: conductance G_i = h_i · ∫ g ds over the edge (h from §8.1 using the cell's upstream fluid-node temperature for properties, lagged) wall temperature T_w,i = Σ_j w_j T_j with w_j = ∫ N_j g ds / ∫ g ds Per cell with upstream fluid node u and downstream node d: G = Σ G_i, T̄_w = Σ G_i T_w,i / G, NTU = G /(ṁ c_p) φ = (1 − e^(−NTU)) / NTU (φ = 1 when NTU < 1e-8) Effective fluid temperature seen by the wall: T_f* = (1 − φ) T̄_w + φ T_u Heat from wall edge i to fluid: Q_i = G_i (T_w,i − T_f*) Fluid energy equation: ṁ c_p (T_d − T_u) − Σ_i Q_i = 0 Q_i is removed from the wall nodes of edge i with the same weights w_j. This scheme is exact for a constant wall temperature per cell, cannot oscillate for any NTU, and conserves energy exactly. The resulting matrix rows are linear in the unknown temperatures (for frozen h and c_p) and unsymmetric . Fluid thermal storage is neglected (quasi-steady fluid) — state this in the user guide. Matrix contributions for one cell, written as a conductance-type matrix K_s such that the heat leaving each DOF is K_s·T: for wall DOF a (weight w_a,i on edge i): row a gets Σ_i w_a,i G_i (T_w,i − (1−φ) T̄_w − φ T_u), and row d gets ṁ c_p (T_d − T_u) − Σ_i G_i (T_w,i − (1−φ) T̄_w − φ T_u). Expand T_w,i and T̄_w into nodal weights to obtain the coefficients. Implement this by building the small dense cell matrix with NumPy and scattering it. A stream may also be through-plane (planar models: flow perpendicular to the model plane, such as a cooling hole seen in cross-section). Then the fluid temperature is uniform on the boundary set and equals the specified bulk temperature; the stream only supplies h from §8.1. No fluid DOFs are created.
docs.title: §9.1 Stream (fluid temperature along a wall)

docs.text: Nodes carry pressure; branches are ducts (§8.1 pressure drop), minor-loss elements, or fixed-flow sources. Boundary conditions: prescribed pressure at a node, or prescribed mass flow into a node. Unknowns: nodal pressures. Branch law: ṁ = sign(Δp) · A √( 2 ρ |Δp| / (f L/D_h + K_minor) ). Linearise as ṁ = c (p_i − p_j) with c = ṁ/Δp from the previous iterate (start with laminar f = 64/Re assumption at Re = 1000). Iterate: assemble Σ c (p_i − p_j) = source at each node, solve, update ṁ and f, under-relax c with factor 0.5, until the largest relative change in any ṁ < 1e-6 (max 200 iterations). Each branch's ṁ then feeds the stream attached to it. Fluid properties in the network use each branch's mean stream temperature; the hydraulic and thermal solutions are alternated inside the nonlinear loop (hydraulics updated at most once per nonlinear iteration, and only when a branch's mean temperature has changed by more than 1 K).
docs.title: §9.2 Network (flow distribution)

docs.text: Not available in this version Enclosure radiation (surface-to-surface radiation, §10 to §10.2) is not implemented in this version (milestone M9 is on hold). The theory is kept here for completeness; no solver module uses it yet. Faces = boundary edge elements of the enclosure, i = 1…n, length-based area A_i = ∫ g ds, emissivity ε_i, face temperature T_i = Σ w_j T_j (weights as in §9.1), E_b,i = σ T_i⁴. View-factor matrix F (n×n). Open enclosures: F_i∞ = 1 − Σ_j F_ij radiates to a black ambient at T_∞. With E = diag(ε): solve (I − (I − E) F) J = E·E_b + (I − E) F_∞ σT_∞⁴ for radiosity J. Net flux leaving face i: q_i = J_i − Σ_j F_ij J_j − F_i∞ σ T_∞⁴. Precompute once per mesh: M = (I − F)(I − (I−E)F)⁻¹ E and the ambient vector. Then q = M E_b + q_∞, heat Q_i = A_i q_i, distributed to the face's nodes with weights w_j. Residual contribution: −Q. Tangent: ∂Q_i/∂T_j = A_i M_ij 4σT_j³ (dense block; insert it fully when n ≤ 3000, otherwise only its diagonal).
docs.title: §10 Enclosure radiation (grey, diffuse)

docs.text: For two straight segments i (endpoints a1,a2) and j (endpoints b1,b2) that fully see each other (Hottel crossed strings): F_ij = [ |a1b2| + |a2b1| − |a1b1| − |a2b2| ] / (2 L_i) (use the absolute value; "crossed" strings are the two that intersect) Visibility: a pair is facing if each midpoint lies on the outward-normal side of the other. A pair is fully visible if facing and none of the four end-to-end sight lines intersects any other enclosure segment. If facing but not fully visible, subdivide both segments into m = 8 sub-segments, apply crossed strings to each fully visible sub-pair (testing sight lines between sub-segment endpoints), and sum: F_ij = Σ_sub L_sub,i F_sub / L_i. Use a uniform grid or shapely.STRtree -free hand-written segment-intersection test vectorised with NumPy. Afterwards enforce reciprocity (A_i F_ij ← ½(A_i F_ij + A_j F_ji)) and, for closed enclosures, scale rows so Σ_j F_ij = 1 (repeat both steps 5 times).
docs.title: §10.1 View factors, planar

docs.text: Each face is a conical ring. Compute F_ij by numerical integration of the 3D kernel cosθ_i cosθ_j /(π r²) over the azimuth of ring j (and sub-divisions of both generators), with blockage tested by intersecting each ray with every other ring's cone frustum. Validate against concentric-cylinder and coaxial-disk closed forms (V-22).
docs.title: §10.2 View factors, axisymmetric (task M9.5)

docs.text: Along an interface curve the mesh has duplicated nodes (one set per side). For each pair of matching edge elements with contact conductance h_c [W/m²·K] add, over the 2n interface DOFs [side A; side B]: K_c = Σ_gp h_c g |J_s| w · [[NᵀN, −NᵀN], [−NᵀN, NᵀN]]
docs.title: §11 Thermal contact resistance

docs.text: Not available in this version Phase change (apparent heat capacity) is not implemented in this version (task M10.2 is on hold). The theory is kept here for completeness; no solver module uses it yet. Latent heat L released between T_sol and T_liq is modelled by replacing ρc with ρc + ρL/(T_liq − T_sol) for T_sol ≤ T ≤ T_liq. Require T_liq − T_sol ≥ 1 K, force lumped capacitance and backward Euler, and limit max_dT_per_step to (T_liq − T_sol)/2.
docs.title: §12 Phase change (apparent heat capacity)

What the units setting does ¶ Choose the units numbers are shown and typed in with Tools > Units.... The dialog has a "Preset" box and one box per quantity. A preset only fills the boxes in; any one of them can be changed afterwards, and the preset box then reads "Custom". The change is one undo step. Units are display units only: The model file ( .tfea ) and the results file store every value in SI, with temperature in kelvin. Changing units changes neither the model nor its results, and makes nothing out of date. Results (plots, read-outs) are shown in the units of the model stored in the results file until you change the units in the session; after that they follow the model. Temperature differences follow the temperature unit (K for K and °C, °F degrees for °F). All conversion factors follow from the exact definitions of the inch, foot, pound, International Table BTU and pound-force. Expressions are always SI ¶ A function given as an expression is evaluated with t in s, x and y in m and T in K, and it returns the SI unit of the quantity, whatever the display units are. The function editor says so when a display unit is not SI. Constants and tables are converted. Places that still show SI only ¶ the HTC calculator window (Tools > HTC calculator...); the solve-progress dialog and the solver messages; the extra parameters of a correlation; CSV and VTU export (the chart CSV, however, follows the display units); the text of thermalfea.api.summary . docs.text: The program is checked against the cases below: each has an analytic or published answer and a tolerance. The tolerances are part of the specification and are never loosened to make a case pass. The computed results are not part of this page. These cases are specified but not active in this version , because the feature they check is on hold: V-22a to V-22d: enclosure radiation (milestone M9, on hold) V-23: enclosure radiation (milestone M9, on hold) V-24: enclosure radiation (milestone M9, on hold) V-36: phase change (task M10.2, on hold) All other cases are active in this version. The cases V-33 and V-37 have no runnable script in examples/ ; they are built inside their tests. V-25 and V-26 are checks of functions, not of a model.
docs.title: Which cases are active

docs.text: Each case becomes one test in tests/verification/test_vNN_*.py and one runnable script in examples/ . Tests compute the analytic answer from the formula given here — do not paste in pre-computed numbers, except the published NAFEMS targets. Unless stated: planar, thickness 1 m, k = 50 W/m·K, ρ = 7800, c = 500, temperatures in K. "1D" cases are modelled as a 2D strip (length L in x, height L/10) with the long sides adiabatic. Run every case with all four element types unless noted. Tolerance is on the relative error against the analytic value, with the mesh size given.

docs.text: Example: main closure of a canned-motor pump ¶ What it is. An axisymmetric model of the bolted main closure between the casing of a canned-motor pump and the main flange of its stator. Hot water inside the casing heats the joint while several cooling circuits take heat away. The model has nine bodies, five sets of convection films and six thermal contacts. It is solved for a six-hour heat-up and for the steady state at full temperature, and a parameter study changes the conductance of the main seat. What it shows. How much heat reaches the flange, by which route, and how the flange temperature develops. It also exercises most of what the program can do on a real assembly: an axisymmetric model, many regions, an orthotropic material, a time-dependent fluid temperature, contact resistances, adaptive time stepping and a scripted parameter study. Illustrative inputs Every dimension, film coefficient, fluid temperature and contact conductance on this page is illustrative. The model is a demonstration of the program and does not represent a particular pump. Unlike the tutorials, this example is built and solved by Python scripts. The scripts, the input file and a complete set of results are in the repository folder examples/pump_closure . Running the example explains how to open the saved results in the program or to run the scripts again. The model ¶ Geometry ¶ The model is a cross-section through the closure in the r-z plane of an axisymmetric model: x is the radius r and y is the axial position z. z = 0 is the joint face between the casing and the flange. Heat flows reported on this page are for the full 360° ring. The program can open and solve an axisymmetric model, but a model created in the window is planar, so this one is built by script. The model (6-node triangles drawn in grey). Coloured edges carry convection films, dotted edges are thermal contacts. Edges with neither are insulated or bonded. Body Extent (mm) Material Casing polygon through (r, z) = (550, 0), (550, 90), (630, 160), (656, 300), (716, 300), (704, 186), (800, 142), (800, 82), (685, 82), (685, 0) Stainless steel 304 Thermal barrier plate r = 120 to 550, z = 48 to 90, with a skirt r = 490 to 550 down to z = 0. A cooling passage of Ø16 mm at (r, z) = (460, 68) is cut out Stainless steel 304 Main flange r = 340 to 800, z = 0 to −150, in three regions: inner (340 to 720), band G (720 to 760) and outer (760 to 800) Stainless steel 304; band G is a mix, below Stud ring D r = 736.8 to 743.2 (6.486 mm wide), z = 0 to 82 Carbon steel AISI 1010 Nut ring N 18.746 mm wide, centred on r = 740, z = −150 to −178 Carbon steel AISI 1010 Stator shell S r = 375 to 435, z = −150 to −330 Stainless steel 304 Liner L r = 260 to 375, z = −150 to −330 Stainless steel 304 The studs and nuts become rings. An axisymmetric model cannot show 24 separate studs. Each row of bolts is replaced by a solid ring with the same total cross-section: a ring of radius R and width w has the area of N bolts of diameter d when 2πR w = N π d²/4. With 24 studs of Ø40 mm on a bolt circle of R = 740 mm, the stud ring is w = 6.486 mm wide. With an equivalent nut diameter of 68 mm, the nut ring is 18.746 mm wide. Inside the flange, the studs are part of band G. Over the 40 mm band from r = 720 to 760 mm, a fraction f = 6.486/40 = 0.162 is carbon-steel stud and the rest is stainless flange. Band G gets a mixed, orthotropic material: along the studs (axial): k = (1 − f) k₃₀₄ + f k₁₀₁₀ (in parallel); across them (radial): k = (1 − f) k₃₀₄, which neglects the studs; density and volumetric heat capacity ρc_p mixed by volume. The material axis is along r, so k is the radial value and k2 the axial one (see Materials for the two library steels). In the r-z model, the heat that goes down the studs therefore enters the flange through band G. Boundary conditions ¶ The five films are convection conditions with a constant heat-transfer coefficient: Film Where h (W/(m² K)) Fluid temperature H hot primary water top and bore of the barrier plate, sloping inner wall of the casing 3000 heat-up: rises linearly from 40 °C to 180 °C over the first 1800 s, then holds; steady case: 180 °C M cooled motor-cavity water underside of the barrier and inside of its skirt, flange ledge and bore, liner ledge and bore 800 55 °C Cw barrier cooling passage the Ø16 mm passage 1500 35 °C J jacket cooling water outer face of the stator shell 1500 35 °C A ambient air outer faces of the casing, the casing lip and the stud cavity, top, rim and underside of the flange 8 30 °C H's fluid temperature in the heat-up is a table against time with two points, (0 s, 40 °C) and (1800 s, 180 °C). A table holds its last value beyond its end. The other edges are insulated (zero heat flux): the two planes where the model is cut off: the top of the casing at z = 300 mm and the bottom of the liner and shell at z = −330 mm; the sides of the stud ring between the flange and the casing lip, and the sides and base of the nut ring. These are short paths to the air in the stud cavity, left out of this run. Thermal contacts ¶ Six interfaces have a contact conductance h_c, so their two sides can be at different temperatures and the heat across them is h_c ΔT per unit area: Contact Between Where h_c (W/(m² K)) Main seat casing and flange z = 0, r = 565 to 685 3000 Seal land casing and flange z = 0, r = 550 to 565 500 Barrier foot barrier skirt and flange z = 0, r = 490 to 550 3000 Vertical fit barrier and casing r = 550, z = 0 to 90 3000 Stud anchor casing lip and stud ring z = 82 5000 Nut bearing nut ring and flange z = −150 5000 All other faces where two bodies meet are bonded, with no resistance. That includes the foot of the stud ring on band G, the boundaries between the three flange regions, and the faces between the liner, the shell and the flange. There are two parallel paths for heat from the casing into the flange: across the seated joint: the seal land, the main seat and the barrier foot; down the studs: from the casing lip across the stud anchor, down stud ring D, and into band G. The nut ring hangs below the flange on its bearing face. It is a dead end: it only exchanges heat while it warms up. Initial state, mesh and solution ¶ Item Value Initial temperature 40 °C everywhere Heat-up transient, 0 to 21 600 s (6 h), first step 1 s, adaptive step, results stored every 300 s (72 steps) Steady hot case steady state with H at 180 °C Mesh 6-node triangles, global element size 10 mm, 1.5 mm along the stud and nut rings, the seal land, the stud anchor, the nut bearing and the cooling passage; 13 037 nodes and 6 188 elements The scripts read every input from closure.json . Change a value there to run a different case. Results ¶ The heat-up ¶ Temperature at six times during the heat-up and at steady state. The last panel is the rise still to come after 6 h. Heat enters along the barrier and the casing wall first. The flange and the studs follow hours later. After 6 h the model is close to, but not at, steady state. The largest rise still to come is 4.4 K, in the outer flange. The heat-up as an animation, written by api.export_animation . A frame every minute for the first hour, then every 5 minutes. All frames use one colour scale. Temperature at 6 h, plotted by api.plot_contour (°C; x = r and y = z in mm). The extremes are 179.2 °C on the casing wall and 35.9 °C on the jacket-cooled stator shell. Temperature in the steady hot case (a steady result is stored at t = 0 s). Heat flows over time ¶ Top: heat through each film. Middle: flange bore and rim temperatures and the mean stud temperature, with the bore-minus-rim difference shaded against the right-hand axis. Bottom: heat across each contact. The hot film peaks at 62 kW as the ramp of H ends at 30 min, then settles towards 35 kW. The flange gradient reverses. The flange bore, cooled by the motor cavity, stays near 51 to 55 °C almost from the start. The rim first cools slightly, to about 39.4 °C, then heats up. The bore is 13.6 K hotter than the rim at 25 min. The two are equal at about 1.5 h, and at 6 h the bore is 39.9 K colder than the rim (44.1 K at steady state). A lumped estimate would give only one sign of this difference. The heat paths peak at different times. Heat across the main seat peaks at 3496 W after about 1.2 h. Heat down the studs (across the stud anchor) peaks at 738 W after about 1.7 h. The vertical fit reverses. For the first hour heat crosses it from the barrier into the casing, at up to about 0.9 kW. It reverses after 1.02 h and ends at 0.81 kW from the casing into the barrier. The same two paths drawn by run_closure.py : the seated joint (seal land and main seat together, peaking near 3.7 kW at about 70 min), the barrier foot, the studs and the nuts. Below is the bore-minus-rim temperature difference. Steady hot case ¶ Quantity Value Heat in through H 35.19 kW Heat out through M, Cw, J, A 21.35, 8.99, 1.48, 3.38 kW Relative energy imbalance 4 × 10⁻¹⁴ Heat into the flange: main seat, seal land, barrier foot, stud anchor 2345, 138, 693, 479 W (3.65 kW in all) Heat across the vertical fit, casing to barrier 855 W Heat across the nut bearing 0 W (to within 3 × 10⁻⁹ W) Flange bore / rim temperature 55.2 °C / 99.3 °C Mean stud temperature 120.2 °C The studs carry 13 % of the heat that enters the flange: 479 W of 3.65 kW. Heat-flux magnitude (logarithmic colour scale) with heat-flow lines in white and isotherms every 20 K in cyan. The right panel zooms in on the joint and the stud ring. The cooling passage is a strong sink. The highest flux, about 88 kW/m², is in the barrier next to the passage. Heat crosses the seated joint and fans out into the flange, and a narrow stream runs down the stud ring. Top: temperature on each side of the joint face z = 0. Bottom: the jump ΔT across each contact. The contacts are real temperature jumps, not smeared bonds. The jump is 1.4 to 3.4 K across the main seat and up to 5.7 K across the seal land, whose conductance is six times lower. Adding up h_c ΔT 2πr along each face gives 2359 W for the main seat, against the solver's 2345 W, and 131 W for the seal land, against 138 W. docs.title: Main closure of a canned-motor pump

docs.text: What it is. An axisymmetric model of the bolted main closure between the casing of a canned-motor pump and the main flange of its stator. Hot water inside the casing heats the joint while several cooling circuits take heat away. The model has nine bodies, five sets of convection films and six thermal contacts. It is solved for a six-hour heat-up and for the steady state at full temperature, and a parameter study changes the conductance of the main seat. What it shows. How much heat reaches the flange, by which route, and how the flange temperature develops. It also exercises most of what the program can do on a real assembly: an axisymmetric model, many regions, an orthotropic material, a time-dependent fluid temperature, contact resistances, adaptive time stepping and a scripted parameter study. Illustrative inputs Every dimension, film coefficient, fluid temperature and contact conductance on this page is illustrative. The model is a demonstration of the program and does not represent a particular pump. Unlike the tutorials, this example is built and solved by Python scripts. The scripts, the input file and a complete set of results are in the repository folder examples/pump_closure . Running the example explains how to open the saved results in the program or to run the scripts again.
docs.title: Example: main closure of a canned-motor pump

docs.text: The model is a cross-section through the closure in the r-z plane of an axisymmetric model: x is the radius r and y is the axial position z. z = 0 is the joint face between the casing and the flange. Heat flows reported on this page are for the full 360° ring. The program can open and solve an axisymmetric model, but a model created in the window is planar, so this one is built by script. The model (6-node triangles drawn in grey). Coloured edges carry convection films, dotted edges are thermal contacts. Edges with neither are insulated or bonded. Body Extent (mm) Material Casing polygon through (r, z) = (550, 0), (550, 90), (630, 160), (656, 300), (716, 300), (704, 186), (800, 142), (800, 82), (685, 82), (685, 0) Stainless steel 304 Thermal barrier plate r = 120 to 550, z = 48 to 90, with a skirt r = 490 to 550 down to z = 0. A cooling passage of Ø16 mm at (r, z) = (460, 68) is cut out Stainless steel 304 Main flange r = 340 to 800, z = 0 to −150, in three regions: inner (340 to 720), band G (720 to 760) and outer (760 to 800) Stainless steel 304; band G is a mix, below Stud ring D r = 736.8 to 743.2 (6.486 mm wide), z = 0 to 82 Carbon steel AISI 1010 Nut ring N 18.746 mm wide, centred on r = 740, z = −150 to −178 Carbon steel AISI 1010 Stator shell S r = 375 to 435, z = −150 to −330 Stainless steel 304 Liner L r = 260 to 375, z = −150 to −330 Stainless steel 304 The studs and nuts become rings. An axisymmetric model cannot show 24 separate studs. Each row of bolts is replaced by a solid ring with the same total cross-section: a ring of radius R and width w has the area of N bolts of diameter d when 2πR w = N π d²/4. With 24 studs of Ø40 mm on a bolt circle of R = 740 mm, the stud ring is w = 6.486 mm wide. With an equivalent nut diameter of 68 mm, the nut ring is 18.746 mm wide. Inside the flange, the studs are part of band G. Over the 40 mm band from r = 720 to 760 mm, a fraction f = 6.486/40 = 0.162 is carbon-steel stud and the rest is stainless flange. Band G gets a mixed, orthotropic material: along the studs (axial): k = (1 − f) k₃₀₄ + f k₁₀₁₀ (in parallel); across them (radial): k = (1 − f) k₃₀₄, which neglects the studs; density and volumetric heat capacity ρc_p mixed by volume. The material axis is along r, so k is the radial value and k2 the axial one (see Materials for the two library steels). In the r-z model, the heat that goes down the studs therefore enters the flange through band G.

docs.text: The five films are convection conditions with a constant heat-transfer coefficient: Film Where h (W/(m² K)) Fluid temperature H hot primary water top and bore of the barrier plate, sloping inner wall of the casing 3000 heat-up: rises linearly from 40 °C to 180 °C over the first 1800 s, then holds; steady case: 180 °C M cooled motor-cavity water underside of the barrier and inside of its skirt, flange ledge and bore, liner ledge and bore 800 55 °C Cw barrier cooling passage the Ø16 mm passage 1500 35 °C J jacket cooling water outer face of the stator shell 1500 35 °C A ambient air outer faces of the casing, the casing lip and the stud cavity, top, rim and underside of the flange 8 30 °C H's fluid temperature in the heat-up is a table against time with two points, (0 s, 40 °C) and (1800 s, 180 °C). A table holds its last value beyond its end. The other edges are insulated (zero heat flux): the two planes where the model is cut off: the top of the casing at z = 300 mm and the bottom of the liner and shell at z = −330 mm; the sides of the stud ring between the flange and the casing lip, and the sides and base of the nut ring. These are short paths to the air in the stud cavity, left out of this run.
docs.title: Boundary conditions

docs.text: Six interfaces have a contact conductance h_c, so their two sides can be at different temperatures and the heat across them is h_c ΔT per unit area: Contact Between Where h_c (W/(m² K)) Main seat casing and flange z = 0, r = 565 to 685 3000 Seal land casing and flange z = 0, r = 550 to 565 500 Barrier foot barrier skirt and flange z = 0, r = 490 to 550 3000 Vertical fit barrier and casing r = 550, z = 0 to 90 3000 Stud anchor casing lip and stud ring z = 82 5000 Nut bearing nut ring and flange z = −150 5000 All other faces where two bodies meet are bonded, with no resistance. That includes the foot of the stud ring on band G, the boundaries between the three flange regions, and the faces between the liner, the shell and the flange. There are two parallel paths for heat from the casing into the flange: across the seated joint: the seal land, the main seat and the barrier foot; down the studs: from the casing lip across the stud anchor, down stud ring D, and into band G. The nut ring hangs below the flange on its bearing face. It is a dead end: it only exchanges heat while it warms up.

docs.text: Top: heat through each film. Middle: flange bore and rim temperatures and the mean stud temperature, with the bore-minus-rim difference shaded against the right-hand axis. Bottom: heat across each contact. The hot film peaks at 62 kW as the ramp of H ends at 30 min, then settles towards 35 kW. The flange gradient reverses. The flange bore, cooled by the motor cavity, stays near 51 to 55 °C almost from the start. The rim first cools slightly, to about 39.4 °C, then heats up. The bore is 13.6 K hotter than the rim at 25 min. The two are equal at about 1.5 h, and at 6 h the bore is 39.9 K colder than the rim (44.1 K at steady state). A lumped estimate would give only one sign of this difference. The heat paths peak at different times. Heat across the main seat peaks at 3496 W after about 1.2 h. Heat down the studs (across the stud anchor) peaks at 738 W after about 1.7 h. The vertical fit reverses. For the first hour heat crosses it from the barrier into the casing, at up to about 0.9 kW. It reverses after 1.02 h and ends at 0.81 kW from the casing into the barrier. The same two paths drawn by run_closure.py : the seated joint (seal land and main seat together, peaking near 3.7 kW at about 70 min), the barrier foot, the studs and the nuts. docs.text: Tutorial 3: a cold plate cooled by a stream of water ¶ What you will build. An aluminium plate that carries 200 W of heat from components on its top face, and a channel of flowing water along its bottom face that carries the heat away. The water is not meshed. It is a stream : a one-dimensional model of the fluid that supplies the heat-transfer coefficient and the water temperature along the wall, and is solved together with the plate. What you will learn. How to create a stream with the New stream dialog; what the path, the flow area, the wetted perimeter and the cross-section are for; how the heat-transfer coefficient follows from the duct correlation; how to read the stream results (outlet temperature, heat picked up, Reynolds number, heat-transfer coefficient, pressure drop); how to check the energy balance by hand; and how the answer changes with the mass flow. The finished model is in models/cold-plate.tfea ; open it with File > Open... to compare with your own. If you have not used the program before, do Tutorial 1 first: it explains the selection procedure used below in detail. The problem ¶ The plate is a strip of 2024-T6 aluminum, 200 mm long, 10 mm thick and 50 mm deep. Components mounted on its top face put 20 kW/m² into it. Over the whole top face that is 20 000 × 0.2 × 0.05 = 200 W . Water at 300 K enters a flat channel along the bottom face and flows from the left end to the right end. The channel is 50 mm wide (as wide as the plate is deep) and 2 mm high. The mass flow is 0.02 kg/s, about 1.2 litres per minute. The two ends of the plate are insulated. The model is a drawing of the plate seen from the side: a rectangle 0.2 m long (x) and 0.01 m tall (y). The depth of 0.05 m is the region "Thickness". The bottom edge is the wall the water touches. The stream does not know the shape of the channel. It is told five things: the flow area A, the cross-section the water flows through: 0.05 m × 0.002 m = 1e-4 m²; the wetted perimeter P, the length of wall around that cross-section: 2 × (0.05 + 0.002) = 0.104 m. With the flow area it gives the hydraulic diameter, D_h = 4 A / P = 3.846 mm; the cross-section type, which selects the laminar Nusselt number. The flat gap is heated from one side (the plate) and insulated on the other (the cover), so the type is parallel_plates_one_side , with Nu = 4.86 for a constant wall temperature (Theory §8.1); the fluid and its inlet temperature ; the path : the polyline the water follows, from inlet to outlet, in the model plane. It tells the program which wall edges are upstream of which. The heat-exchange area is taken from the model: the length of the wall edge times the region thickness, 0.2 m × 0.05 m = 0.01 m². It agrees with the channel because the channel is as wide as the plate is deep. Item Value Geometry rectangle 0.2 m (x) by 0.01 m (y); depth 0.05 m ("Thickness" of the region) Material Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6, from the library: k = 177 W/(m K) Heat flux on the top edge 20 000 W/m², into the plate (200 W in all) Left and right edges adiabatic Fluid Water, inlet temperature 300 K, mass flow 0.02 kg/s Flow area / wetted perimeter 1e-4 m² / 0.104 m Cross-section parallel_plates_one_side Path from (0, 0) to (0.2, 0), along the bottom edge Wall the bottom edge Mesh global element size 0.005 m (126 nodes, 166 elements) Analysis steady The water properties (density 996.6 kg/m³, viscosity 8.537e-4 Pa s, conductivity 0.6095 W/(m K), specific heat 4181 J/(kg K) at 300 K) come from the library table for water, which covers 280 K to 370 K. The water here stays between 300 K and 302.4 K, so the program does not warn. Temperature units. Everything is in kelvin, the default. Steps ¶ 1. Draw the geometry ¶ Choose Geometry > Rectangle... . Type x = 0 , y = 0 , Width = 0.2 , Height = 0.01 and press OK . The status bar shows "Building geometry..." and then "Geometry rebuilt". Choose View > Fit view (or press F ). The plate is twenty times longer than tall, so it is a thin band on screen. Zoom with the mouse wheel if you cannot hit the edges later. A middle-button drag pans. 2. Take the material from the library ¶ Choose Tools > Material library... . On the Built-in tab select Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6 and press Copy into model . A node "Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6" appears under Materials . Close the window. 3. Assign it to the plate ¶ Right-click Regions and choose Add region . The panel "Region" opens. Open the box of the "Selection" field and choose all (every surface of the model, here the one plate). "Material" already reads "Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6". In "Thickness" type 0.05 and press Enter. 4. Enter the loads ¶ The heat flux of the components. Right-click Loads & Boundary Conditions and choose Add > Add Heat Flux . The node "Heat Flux 1" appears and its panel opens. In "Selection" press Pick in viewport , choose Curve in the toolbar, click the top edge ("1 curve(s) picked"), press Apply and switch picking off. In "Heat flux" type 20000 and press Enter (W/m²). A positive flux heats the plate. Insulated ends. Right-click Loads & Boundary Conditions and choose Add > Add Adiabatic . In "Selection" pick the left edge, Ctrl -click the right edge ("2 curve(s) picked"), press Apply and switch picking off. The bottom edge gets no load. It belongs to the stream, which you add next. 5. Create the stream ¶ In the tree, open Flow . Right-click the node Streams and choose Add stream . Because the model has no stream yet, a window titled "New stream" opens. It says "The model has no stream yet. Enter the values of the first one." Its fields start empty, so no value is assumed. Fill in: Field Value Fluid Water Flow area [m^2] 1e-4 Wetted perimeter [m] 0.104 Cross-section parallel_plates_one_side Inlet temperature [K] 300 Press Create . If a field is empty, the window stays open and says which one ("enter the flow area", "choose a fluid", ...). When it closes, a node Stream 1 appears under Streams and its panel "Stream: Stream 1" opens. The mode is in_plane : the water flows along a path in the plane of the drawing. (The other mode, through_plane , is for flow perpendicular to the drawing, such as a cooling hole seen in cross-section.) The dialog only asks for the values every stream needs. The rest are in the panel, which you now complete. 6. Complete the stream ¶ Walls. In the "Walls" field press Pick in viewport , choose Curve in the toolbar, click the bottom edge ("1 curve(s) picked"), press Apply and switch picking off. The field now lists "Stream 1 walls". This is the edge the water cools. Path. In "Path" type 0, 0; 0.2, 0 and press Enter. The format is x, y; x, y , one pair per point, in metres. The label under the "Path" buttons reads "2 path points". (You may instead press Pick path points and click the inlet and then the outlet in the viewport. The clicks are not exact, so typing is better here.) The path runs along the wall from the inlet end to the outlet end. Mass flow. The box "Mass flow" shows the mode Constant and the value 0, although no mass flow has been set yet. Type 0.02 and press Enter (kg/s). (Leave the field empty only when a flow network supplies the flow.) Leave the rest as it is: "Wall roughness" 0 (smooth), "Number of cells" empty (one fluid cell per wall edge along the path, which is 40 here), "Nusselt option" auto (laminar table, Gnielinski for turbulent flow), "Coefficient multiplier" 1 and "Coefficient override" empty. 7. Mesh and solve ¶ Click the node Mesh . In "Global element size" type 0.005 and press Enter. Press Generate mesh . The mesh panel lists 126 nodes and 166 elements. Choose Solve > Validate . The status bar says "Validation: no issues". Choose Solve > Solve . The analysis is steady (the default), but nonlinear, because the heat-transfer coefficient and the fluid properties depend on temperature. The "Solving" window shows 3 iterations. The status bar reads "Solve finished ... 1 stored step(s)". (For a steady solution the time shown is a placeholder, "t = 0 s".) The unknowns are the plate temperatures and the water temperature at the 41 fluid nodes of the stream, solved together in one system. 8. Read the stream results ¶ Choose Results > Flow results... . (It is greyed out unless the results contain a stream.) A window titled "Flow results" opens with one row per stream: Stream Mode Mass flow [kg/s] Re Regime Mean h [W/(m^2 K)] dp [Pa] T_in [K] T_out [K] Heat [W] Stream 1 in_plane 0.02 923.245 laminar 772.433 72.3679 300 302.392 200 "Heat" is the heat the water picks up from the wall. "Mean h" is the average of the coefficient over the cells. 2. Select the row and press Plot . A chart window shows the water temperature and the mean wall temperature against the distance along the path. 3. The temperature field is drawn in the viewport. Choose Results > Probe and click it to read single values, or use File > Export > Nodal results (CSV)... . 4. Results > Heat-flow history and the "Messages" dock list the heat entering through each condition: Heat Flux 1 gives +200 W and Stream 1 gives -200 W. Results ¶ Quantity Value Water outlet temperature 302.39 K (rise 2.39 K) Heat picked up by the water 200.0 W Reynolds number 923 (laminar) Mean heat-transfer coefficient 772.4 W/(m² K) Pressure drop 72.4 Pa Hottest point of the plate 328.82 K Coolest point of the plate 326.49 K The plate is hottest at the outlet end of the top face, where the water is warmest, and coolest at the inlet end of the bottom face. The whole plate lies within 2.5 K, because the aluminium conducts well compared with the water film. Most of the temperature difference between the plate and the water is across the film (step 7 of the hand check below). Checking the answer ¶ By hand ¶ Use the water properties of the library at 300 K, as listed above. Hydraulic diameter. D_h = 4 A / P = 4 × 1e-4 / 0.104 = 3.846 mm. Velocity. V = ṁ / (ρ A) = 0.02 / (996.6 × 1e-4) = 0.2007 m/s. Reynolds number. Re = ṁ D_h / (A μ) = 0.02 × 3.846e-3 / (1e-4 × 8.537e-4) = 901 . This is below 2300, so the flow is laminar. The program reports 923.2. It takes the properties at the local water temperature, 300 K to 302.4 K, and the viscosity falls as the water warms, so its Reynolds number is 2.5 % higher. Heat-transfer coefficient. For laminar flow the Nusselt number is the table value, 4.86. h = Nu k / D_h = 4.86 × 0.6095 / 3.846e-3 = 770.2 W/(m² K) . The program's mean is 772.4, 0.3 % higher, for the same reason. Heat load. Q = q L depth = 20 000 × 0.2 × 0.05 = 200 W . Outlet temperature. ṁ c_p ΔT = Q gives ΔT = 200 / (0.02 × 4180.64) = 2.392 K , so T_out = 302.392 K. The program gives 302.392 K: it takes c_p at the inlet temperature, exactly as in this calculation. Wall above the water. The bottom edge carries the same flux density as the top edge, so the wall is q / h above the water: 20 000 / 770.2 = 26.0 K . In the model, the mean wall temperature at mid-length is 25.89 K above the water temperature there. Pressure drop. Δp = f (L / D_h) ρ V² / 2. For laminar flow f is close to 64 / Re (Theory §9.2 uses it as the starting value of its flow iteration), here 64 / 901 = 0.0710. With L / D_h = 0.2 / 3.846e-3 = 52.0 and ρ V² / 2 = 20.07 Pa, Δp ≈ 74.1 Pa. The program gives 72.4 Pa, using the Reynolds number above and its own friction formula (Churchill, in Theory §8.1). The two differ by 2 %, which is the difference in the Reynolds number. Energy balance ¶ The 200 W that enter through Heat Flux 1 must leave with the water: heat in equals ṁ c_p (T_out − T_in). Both sides are 200 W. The program checks this at every solve: the relative imbalance of this case is about 1e-13, far below the limit of 1e-3 for nonlinear cases (verification case V-29 sets the same check for streams, to 1e-8). You can read it at the end of the log in the "Messages" dock, under "relative imbalance". What if the mass flow changes? ¶ Click the node Stream 1 . In "Mass flow" type 0.1 and press Enter. The result panel now says "These results are out of date: the model changed since the solve." (Click the result node under Solution to see it.) The mesh is still valid. Choose Solve > Solve again. The "Flow results" window, if still open, shows the new numbers when the solve finishes. Repeat with 0.005 . Mass flow [kg/s] Re Regime Mean h [W/(m² K)] Δp [Pa] T_out [K] Hottest point of the plate [K] 0.005 249 laminar 779.2 16.8 309.57 334.06 0.02 923 laminar 772.4 72.4 302.39 328.82 0.1 4527 turbulent 5398 1019 300.48 305.26 The heat picked up is 200 W in all three cases: it is set by the components, not by the water. What changes is how warm the water gets and how hot the plate runs. Between 0.005 and 0.02 kg/s the flow is laminar. The Nusselt number is a constant of the cross-section, so h barely changes (it changes a little because the water properties change). A faster flow lowers the outlet temperature (309.57 K to 302.39 K) and so the plate temperature, but only through the water temperature: the difference between the wall and the water at mid-length stays at about 26 K (25.6 K and 25.9 K). At 0.1 kg/s the Reynolds number, 4527, is above 4000 and the program switches to the turbulent correlation (Gnielinski, Theory §8.1). The coefficient rises by a factor of seven and the difference between the wall and the water at mid-length falls from about 26 K to 3.7 K. The plate runs at 305.3 K instead of 328.8 K. The price is a pressure drop 14 times as large: 1019 Pa against 72.4 Pa. Between Reynolds numbers of 2300 and 4000 the program interpolates between the laminar and the turbulent values, so h rises smoothly through the transition. Things to try ¶ Change "Cross-section" in the stream panel to parallel_plates (heated on both sides) and see how the laminar h changes: the table gives 7.54 against 4.86. Give "Wall roughness" a value and compare the pressure drop at 0.1 kg/s. Type a value in "Coefficient override" to replace the correlation with a fixed h, and compare the plate temperature with the correlation result. Set "Number of cells" to 10 and compare the outlet temperature and the plate temperature with the 40-cell result. docs.title: Cold plate with a water stream

docs.text: What you will build. An aluminium plate that carries 200 W of heat from components on its top face, and a channel of flowing water along its bottom face that carries the heat away. The water is not meshed. It is a stream : a one-dimensional model of the fluid that supplies the heat-transfer coefficient and the water temperature along the wall, and is solved together with the plate. What you will learn. How to create a stream with the New stream dialog; what the path, the flow area, the wetted perimeter and the cross-section are for; how the heat-transfer coefficient follows from the duct correlation; how to read the stream results (outlet temperature, heat picked up, Reynolds number, heat-transfer coefficient, pressure drop); how to check the energy balance by hand; and how the answer changes with the mass flow. The finished model is in models/cold-plate.tfea ; open it with File > Open... to compare with your own. If you have not used the program before, do Tutorial 1 first: it explains the selection procedure used below in detail.
docs.title: Tutorial 3: a cold plate cooled by a stream of water

docs.text: The plate is a strip of 2024-T6 aluminum, 200 mm long, 10 mm thick and 50 mm deep. Components mounted on its top face put 20 kW/m² into it. Over the whole top face that is 20 000 × 0.2 × 0.05 = 200 W . Water at 300 K enters a flat channel along the bottom face and flows from the left end to the right end. The channel is 50 mm wide (as wide as the plate is deep) and 2 mm high. The mass flow is 0.02 kg/s, about 1.2 litres per minute. The two ends of the plate are insulated. The model is a drawing of the plate seen from the side: a rectangle 0.2 m long (x) and 0.01 m tall (y). The depth of 0.05 m is the region "Thickness". The bottom edge is the wall the water touches. The stream does not know the shape of the channel. It is told five things: the flow area A, the cross-section the water flows through: 0.05 m × 0.002 m = 1e-4 m²; the wetted perimeter P, the length of wall around that cross-section: 2 × (0.05 + 0.002) = 0.104 m. With the flow area it gives the hydraulic diameter, D_h = 4 A / P = 3.846 mm; the cross-section type, which selects the laminar Nusselt number. The flat gap is heated from one side (the plate) and insulated on the other (the cover), so the type is parallel_plates_one_side , with Nu = 4.86 for a constant wall temperature (Theory §8.1); the fluid and its inlet temperature ; the path : the polyline the water follows, from inlet to outlet, in the model plane. It tells the program which wall edges are upstream of which. The heat-exchange area is taken from the model: the length of the wall edge times the region thickness, 0.2 m × 0.05 m = 0.01 m². It agrees with the channel because the channel is as wide as the plate is deep. Item Value Geometry rectangle 0.2 m (x) by 0.01 m (y); depth 0.05 m ("Thickness" of the region) Material Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6, from the library: k = 177 W/(m K) Heat flux on the top edge 20 000 W/m², into the plate (200 W in all) Left and right edges adiabatic Fluid Water, inlet temperature 300 K, mass flow 0.02 kg/s Flow area / wetted perimeter 1e-4 m² / 0.104 m Cross-section parallel_plates_one_side Path from (0, 0) to (0.2, 0), along the bottom edge Wall the bottom edge Mesh global element size 0.005 m (126 nodes, 166 elements) Analysis steady The water properties (density 996.6 kg/m³, viscosity 8.537e-4 Pa s, conductivity 0.6095 W/(m K), specific heat 4181 J/(kg K) at 300 K) come from the library table for water, which covers 280 K to 370 K. The water here stays between 300 K and 302.4 K, so the program does not warn. Temperature units. Everything is in kelvin, the default.
docs.title: The problem

docs.text: Choose Geometry > Rectangle... . Type x = 0 , y = 0 , Width = 0.2 , Height = 0.01 and press OK . The status bar shows "Building geometry..." and then "Geometry rebuilt". Choose View > Fit view (or press F ). The plate is twenty times longer than tall, so it is a thin band on screen. Zoom with the mouse wheel if you cannot hit the edges later. A middle-button drag pans.
docs.title: 1. Draw the geometry

docs.text: Choose Tools > Material library... . On the Built-in tab select Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6 and press Copy into model . A node "Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6" appears under Materials . Close the window.
docs.title: 2. Take the material from the library

docs.text: Right-click Regions and choose Add region . The panel "Region" opens. Open the box of the "Selection" field and choose all (every surface of the model, here the one plate). "Material" already reads "Aluminum, Alloy 2024-T6". In "Thickness" type 0.05 and press Enter.
docs.title: 3. Assign it to the plate

docs.text: The heat flux of the components. Right-click Loads & Boundary Conditions and choose Add > Add Heat Flux . The node "Heat Flux 1" appears and its panel opens. In "Selection" press Pick in viewport , choose Curve in the toolbar, click the top edge ("1 curve(s) picked"), press Apply and switch picking off. In "Heat flux" type 20000 and press Enter (W/m²). A positive flux heats the plate. Insulated ends. Right-click Loads & Boundary Conditions and choose Add > Add Adiabatic . In "Selection" pick the left edge, Ctrl -click the right edge ("2 curve(s) picked"), press Apply and switch picking off. The bottom edge gets no load. It belongs to the stream, which you add next.
docs.title: 4. Enter the loads

docs.text: In the tree, open Flow . Right-click the node Streams and choose Add stream . Because the model has no stream yet, a window titled "New stream" opens. It says "The model has no stream yet. Enter the values of the first one." Its fields start empty, so no value is assumed. Fill in: Field Value Fluid Water Flow area [m^2] 1e-4 Wetted perimeter [m] 0.104 Cross-section parallel_plates_one_side Inlet temperature [K] 300 Press Create . If a field is empty, the window stays open and says which one ("enter the flow area", "choose a fluid", ...). When it closes, a node Stream 1 appears under Streams and its panel "Stream: Stream 1" opens. The mode is in_plane : the water flows along a path in the plane of the drawing. (The other mode, through_plane , is for flow perpendicular to the drawing, such as a cooling hole seen in cross-section.) The dialog only asks for the values every stream needs. The rest are in the panel, which you now complete.
docs.title: 5. Create the stream

docs.text: Walls. In the "Walls" field press Pick in viewport , choose Curve in the toolbar, click the bottom edge ("1 curve(s) picked"), press Apply and switch picking off. The field now lists "Stream 1 walls". This is the edge the water cools. Path. In "Path" type 0, 0; 0.2, 0 and press Enter. The format is x, y; x, y , one pair per point, in metres. The label under the "Path" buttons reads "2 path points". (You may instead press Pick path points and click the inlet and then the outlet in the viewport. The clicks are not exact, so typing is better here.) The path runs along the wall from the inlet end to the outlet end. Mass flow. The box "Mass flow" shows the mode Constant and the value 0, although no mass flow has been set yet. Type 0.02 and press Enter (kg/s). (Leave the field empty only when a flow network supplies the flow.) Leave the rest as it is: "Wall roughness" 0 (smooth), "Number of cells" empty (one fluid cell per wall edge along the path, which is 40 here), "Nusselt option" auto (laminar table, Gnielinski for turbulent flow), "Coefficient multiplier" 1 and "Coefficient override" empty.
docs.title: 6. Complete the stream

docs.text: Click the node Mesh . In "Global element size" type 0.005 and press Enter. Press Generate mesh . The mesh panel lists 126 nodes and 166 elements. Choose Solve > Validate . The status bar says "Validation: no issues". Choose Solve > Solve . The analysis is steady (the default), but nonlinear, because the heat-transfer coefficient and the fluid properties depend on temperature. The "Solving" window shows 3 iterations. The status bar reads "Solve finished ... 1 stored step(s)". (For a steady solution the time shown is a placeholder, "t = 0 s".) The unknowns are the plate temperatures and the water temperature at the 41 fluid nodes of the stream, solved together in one system.
docs.title: 7. Mesh and solve

docs.text: Choose Results > Flow results... . (It is greyed out unless the results contain a stream.) A window titled "Flow results" opens with one row per stream: Stream Mode Mass flow [kg/s] Re Regime Mean h [W/(m^2 K)] dp [Pa] T_in [K] T_out [K] Heat [W] Stream 1 in_plane 0.02 923.245 laminar 772.433 72.3679 300 302.392 200 "Heat" is the heat the water picks up from the wall. "Mean h" is the average of the coefficient over the cells. 2. Select the row and press Plot . A chart window shows the water temperature and the mean wall temperature against the distance along the path. 3. The temperature field is drawn in the viewport. Choose Results > Probe and click it to read single values, or use File > Export > Nodal results (CSV)... . 4. Results > Heat-flow history and the "Messages" dock list the heat entering through each condition: Heat Flux 1 gives +200 W and Stream 1 gives -200 W.
docs.title: 8. Read the stream results

docs.text: Quantity Value Water outlet temperature 302.39 K (rise 2.39 K) Heat picked up by the water 200.0 W Reynolds number 923 (laminar) Mean heat-transfer coefficient 772.4 W/(m² K) Pressure drop 72.4 Pa Hottest point of the plate 328.82 K Coolest point of the plate 326.49 K The plate is hottest at the outlet end of the top face, where the water is warmest, and coolest at the inlet end of the bottom face. The whole plate lies within 2.5 K, because the aluminium conducts well compared with the water film. Most of the temperature difference between the plate and the water is across the film (step 7 of the hand check below).
